quiz.q: Two figures are congruent if one can be mapped onto the other using:
quiz.explanation: Congruent figures can be mapped onto each other using any combination of rigid motions (translations, reflections, and rotations), which preserve size and shape.

lessons.title: Triangle Congruence Postulates
lessons.description: Learn SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, and HL congruence criteria.
lessons.formula:
Triangle Congruence Criteria:
• SSS (Side-Side-Side): If 3 sides of one Δ ≡ 3 sides of another Δ
• SAS (Side-Angle-Side): If 2 sides + included angle of one Δ ≡ those of another Δ
• ASA (Angle-Side-Angle): If 2 angles + included side of one Δ ≡ those of another Δ
• AAS (Angle-Angle-Side): If 2 angles + non-included side of one Δ ≡ those of another Δ
• HL (Hypotenuse-Leg): If hypotenuse + 1 leg of one right Δ ≡ those of another right Δ

WARNING: SSA and AAA do NOT prove congruence!
lessons.content:
Triangle congruence postulates provide efficient shortcuts for proving two triangles are congruent without checking all six corresponding parts. Instead of verifying three sides and three angles individually, these postulates require only three specific pieces of information arranged in a particular order. The SSS Postulate states that if all three sides of one triangle are congruent to the three sides of another, the triangles are congruent.

The SAS Postulate requires two sides and the included angle (the angle between those two sides) to be congruent. The ASA Postulate requires two angles and the included side (the side between those angles). The AAS Postulate requires two angles and a non-included side. For right triangles specifically, the HL (Hypotenuse-Leg) Theorem states that if the hypotenuse and one leg of one right triangle are congruent to those of another, the triangles are congruent.

Two common traps to avoid: SSA (Side-Side-Angle) and AAA (Angle-Angle-Angle) do not guarantee congruence. SSA can produce two different triangles (the ambiguous case), and AAA only tells you the triangles are similar (same shape, possibly different size). Always identify which postulate applies by checking the arrangement of given parts: the included elements must match the postulate's pattern.
steps: List all the given information about both triangles (sides and angles marked congruent)
Determine which pairs of corresponding parts are congruent
Check if the congruent parts match one of the five postulates: SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, or HL
Verify that the angle in SAS is the included angle between the two sides
Verify that the side in ASA is the included side between the two angles
State the congruence statement and cite the postulate as your reason

examples.title: Example 1: Proving Congruence with SAS
examples.text:
In ΔABC and ΔDEF: AB ≡ DE, ∠B ≡ ∠E, and BC ≡ EF.

Step 1: Two sides are congruent: AB ≡ DE and BC ≡ EF
Step 2: The included angle between them is congruent: ∠B ≡ ∠E
Step 3: The pattern is Side-Angle-Side (SAS)
Step 4: ΔABC ≡ ΔDEF by SAS
Note: ∠B is between sides AB and BC, and ∠E is between sides DE and EF.

examples.title: Example 2: Identifying the Wrong Postulate (SSA Trap)
examples.text:
In ΔPQR and ΔSTU: PQ ≡ ST, PR ≡ SU, and ∠Q ≡ ∠T. Can we prove congruence?

Step 1: We have Side (PQ ≡ ST), Side (PR ≡ SU), and Angle (∠Q ≡ ∠T).
Step 2: ∠Q is NOT the included angle between PQ and PR (that would be ∠P).
Step 3: The angle is non-included, making this SSA, which is NOT a valid congruence postulate.
Conclusion: We cannot prove ΔPQR ≡ ΔSTU with the given information.

lessons.tip: Draw both triangles side by side with the same orientation, marking congruent parts with the same number of tick marks (for sides) and arc marks (for angles). This visual makes it easy to see if you have SSS, SAS, ASA, or AAS. If the angle is between two sides, it's SAS; if not, check whether it's AAS or the invalid SSA.

quiz.q: Which congruence postulate requires two angles and the side between them?
quiz.explanation: ASA (Angle-Side-Angle) requires two angles and the included side — the side that lies between those two angles.

quiz.q: Why does AAA not prove triangle congruence?
options: Because angles can never be measured accurately
Because it only guarantees similarity, not equal size
Because three angles always sum to 180°
Because it violates the triangle inequality
quiz.explanation: AAA tells us the triangles have the same shape (are similar), but they could be different sizes. We need at least one side to establish equal size for congruence.

quiz.q: The HL theorem can only be used to prove congruence between:
quiz.explanation: The Hypotenuse-Leg (HL) theorem applies specifically to right triangles, using the hypotenuse and one leg as the congruent parts.

lessons.title: CPCTC
lessons.description: Use Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent.
lessons.formula:
CPCTC: Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent

If ΔABC ≡ ΔDEF, then:
• ∠A ≡ ∠D
• ∠B ≡ ∠E
• ∠C ≡ ∠F
• AB ≡ DE
• BC ≡ EF
• AC ≡ DF

Usage flow:
1. Prove triangles congruent (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL)
2. State CPCTC
3. Conclude specific parts are congruent
lessons.content:
CPCTC stands for "Corresponding Parts of Congruent Triangles are Congruent." This powerful principle states that once you have proven two triangles congruent using one of the five postulates (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, or HL), you can immediately conclude that every pair of corresponding parts is congruent. CPCTC is not a way to prove triangles congruent — it is a conclusion you draw after establishing congruence.

In practice, CPCTC is the bridge between proving two triangles are congruent and solving the actual problem you were asked about. For example, if a question asks you to prove that two segments are equal, your strategy would be to (1) identify two triangles that contain those segments, (2) prove the triangles are congruent using a valid postulate, and (3) apply CPCTC to conclude the segments are congruent. This three-step approach is the most common proof structure in geometry.

In a two-column proof, CPCTC always appears as a reason in a statement about a specific side or angle being congruent. It typically comes near the end of the proof, after you have already established triangle congruence. When using CPCTC, make sure to state the full congruence statement first (which pairs of triangles are congruent) and then identify which specific corresponding parts you are concluding are congruent. The order of vertices in your congruence statement determines which parts correspond.
steps: Identify what you need to prove (e.g., two segments or angles are congruent)
Find two triangles that contain the parts you need to prove congruent
Gather given information and mark congruent parts on both triangles
Prove the two triangles are congruent using SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, or HL
State CPCTC as the reason for the congruence of the specific parts you need
Write your final conclusion based on the CPCTC result

examples.title: Example 1: Proving Segments Equal Using CPCTC
examples.text:
Given: AB ∥ DC, AB ≡ DC. Prove: AD ≡ BC.

Step 1: Draw diagonal AC to create ΔABC and ΔCDA.
Step 2: AB ≡ DC (given)
Step 3: ∠BAC ≡ ∠DCA (alternate interior angles, AB ∥ DC)
Step 4: AC ≡ AC (reflexive property)
Step 5: ΔABC ≡ ΔCDA by SAS
Step 6: AD ≡ BC by CPCTC
Done! We proved the segments are equal.

examples.title: Example 2: Proving Angles Equal Using CPCTC
examples.text:
Given: E is the midpoint of AC and BD, and ∠AEB ≡ ∠CED. Prove: ∠ABE ≡ ∠CDE.

Step 1: AE ≡ CE and BE ≡ DE (midpoint definition)
Step 2: ∠AEB ≡ ∠CED (given)
Step 3: ΔAEB ≡ ΔCED by SAS (AE ≡ CE, ∠AEB ≡ ∠CED, BE ≡ DE)
Step 4: ∠ABE ≡ ∠CDE by CPCTC
The two angles are congruent.

lessons.tip: Think of CPCTC as a two-stage rocket: Stage 1 gets you to triangle congruence (using SSS, SAS, etc.), and Stage 2 (CPCTC) gets you to your final destination (congruent parts). Always know which stage you are in before you write your next statement.

quiz.q: CPCTC is used to:
options: Find the area of a triangle
Conclude specific parts are congruent after proving triangles congruent
quiz.explanation: CPCTC is used AFTER proving two triangles are congruent to then conclude that their corresponding parts (sides and angles) are also congruent.

quiz.q: In a proof, CPCTC typically appears:
options: At the beginning of the proof
In the middle, before establishing triangle congruence
Near the end, after proving triangles congruent
quiz.explanation: CPCTC is applied after you have already proven triangle congruence, so it appears near the end of the proof as a reason for concluding parts are congruent.

quiz.q: If ΔJKL ≡ ΔMNO by SSS, which statement is justified by CPCTC?
quiz.explanation: CPCTC tells us that corresponding angles are congruent: ∠J ≡ ∠M (the first vertices in each triangle). The triangle congruence itself was already established by SSS.

lessons.title: Congruence Proofs
lessons.description: Write complete two-column proofs for triangle congruence.
lessons.formula:
Common Proof Reasons:
• Given — information stated in the problem
• Definition of midpoint — divides a segment into 2 equal parts
• Vertical angles are congruent
• Alternate interior angles ≡ (lines parallel)
• Reflexive property — any quantity = itself
• Symmetric property — if a = b, then b = a
• Transitive property — if a = b and b = c, then a = c
• Substitution — replace equal values in an expression
• SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL — congruence postulates
• CPCTC — corresponding parts of ≡ triangles are ≡
lessons.content:
Congruence proofs are formal arguments that use logic and geometric properties to demonstrate that two triangles are congruent and then to draw conclusions about their corresponding parts. The standard format is the two-column proof, where every statement on the left has a matching reason on the right. Mastering this format is essential for success in geometry and builds critical thinking skills that transfer to advanced mathematics.

A typical congruence proof follows a predictable pattern: (1) identify the triangles to be proven congruent, (2) mark all given congruent parts, (3) use definitions and theorems to establish additional congruent parts, (4) apply one of the five congruence postulates (SSS, SAS, ASA, AAS, HL), and (5) use CPCTC to conclude the specific parts requested. Common supporting reasons include the definition of midpoint, the vertical angles theorem, the reflexive property (a shared side equals itself), and various parallel line angle relationships.

The key to writing effective proofs is working backward from what you need to prove. If you need to prove two sides equal, ask yourself: "Which two triangles contain these sides?" and "What do I need to prove those triangles congruent?" Then work forward from the givens to fill in the missing pieces. Common strategies include drawing auxiliary lines (like diagonals in quadrilaterals), using the reflexive property for shared sides, and leveraging angle relationships from parallel lines or vertical angles.
steps: Read the problem and identify what needs to be proved
Draw and label a diagram, marking all given information with tick marks and arcs
Identify the two triangles you plan to prove congruent
List the congruent parts you already know from the givens
Determine what additional congruent parts you need for a valid postulate
Use theorems and properties to establish those additional parts, then state the congruence postulate and apply CPCTC

examples.title: Example 1: Proof Using Overlapping Triangles
examples.text:
Given: AB ≡ CD, AB ∥ CD. Prove: ΔABD ≡ ΔCDB.

Statements:                      Reasons:
1. AB ≡ CD                      1. Given
2. AB ∥ CD                     2. Given
3. ∠ABD ≡ ∠CDB             3. Alt. int. angles (∥ lines)
4. BD ≡ BD                     4. Reflexive property
5. ΔABD ≡ ΔCDB             5. SAS (Steps 1, 3, 4)

examples.title: Example 2: Proof Using a Diagonal in a Quadrilateral
examples.text:
Given: QRST is a rectangle, QS is a diagonal. Prove: ΔQRS ≡ ΔSTQ.

Statements:                          Reasons:
1. QRST is a rectangle              1. Given
2. QR ≡ ST and ∠Q = ∠S = 90° 2. Properties of a rectangle
3. QS ≡ QS                        3. Reflexive property
4. ΔQRS ≡ ΔSTQ                4. SAS (Steps 2-3)
5. RS ≡ TQ                        5. CPCTC

lessons.tip: When working with overlapping triangles, redraw them as two separate triangles side by side. This makes it much easier to see which parts are shared and which are corresponding. Use different colors for the shared and non-shared parts.

quiz.q: In a two-column proof, the 'reflexive property' is commonly used to justify that:
options: A shared side of two triangles is congruent to itself
quiz.explanation: The reflexive property states that any quantity equals itself. In proofs, it is most commonly used to show that a shared side (like segment BD in ΔABD and ΔCBD) is congruent to itself.

quiz.q: What is the first step in planning a congruence proof?
options: Identify which triangles to prove congruent
quiz.explanation: Before you can prove anything, you must first identify the two triangles you plan to prove congruent, as everything else in the proof revolves around those triangles.

quiz.q: Which property justifies: 'If AB ≡ CD and CD ≡ EF, then AB ≡ EF'?
quiz.explanation: The transitive property states that if a = b and b = c, then a = c. Applied to congruence: if AB ≡ CD and CD ≡ EF, then AB ≡ EF.

lessons.title: Similar Polygons
lessons.description: Understand similarity and solve problems with similar figures.
lessons.formula:
Similar Polygons:
Corresponding angles are congruent.
Corresponding sides are proportional.

Scale Factor (k):
k = (side of image) / (side of pre-image)
All corresponding side ratios equal k.

If polygon A ~ polygon B with scale factor k:
• Perimeter ratio = k
• Area ratio = k²

Example: k = 3/2 means the image is 1.5 times larger.
Area of image = (9/4) × Area of pre-image.
lessons.content:
Similar polygons have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Two polygons are similar (written with the ~ symbol) if and only if two conditions are met: (1) all pairs of corresponding angles are congruent, and (2) all pairs of corresponding sides are proportional. Both conditions must hold simultaneously — having only congruent angles or only proportional sides is not sufficient.

The ratio of lengths of corresponding sides is called the scale factor (often denoted k). If the scale factor is, say, 2:3, every side of the first polygon is 2/3 the length of the corresponding side of the second polygon. When working with proportions, set up ratios of corresponding sides and solve for unknown lengths. For example, if AB/DE = BC/EF, and you know three of these values, you can find the fourth.

An important consequence of similarity is how it affects perimeter and area. The ratio of perimeters of similar figures equals the scale factor k, but the ratio of areas equals k². So if one figure has sides three times as long as another, its area is nine times as large. This principle is widely used in map reading, architectural models, and engineering where scale drawings and models represent real-world objects at reduced or enlarged sizes.
steps: Identify the two polygons and list their corresponding vertices in order
Verify that all corresponding angles are congruent
Write the ratios of corresponding sides as a proportion
Calculate the scale factor from the known side lengths
Use the scale factor to find any unknown side lengths
For area problems, remember that the area ratio is the square of the scale factor

examples.title: Example 1: Finding a Missing Side in Similar Polygons
examples.text:
Rectangle ABCD ~ Rectangle EFGH. AB = 5, BC = 8, EF = 15. Find FG.

Step 1: The scale factor is EF/AB = 15/5 = 3
Step 2: Since the rectangles are similar, all corresponding sides have the same scale factor.
Step 3: FG = BC × k = 8 × 3 = 24
Alternatively, set up a proportion: 5/15 = 8/FG → 5(FG) = 120 → FG = 24

examples.title: Example 2: Scale Factor and Area
examples.text:
Two similar trapezoids have a scale factor of 2:5 (smaller to larger). The smaller trapezoid has an area of 36 cm². Find the area of the larger trapezoid.

Step 1: Scale factor k = 5/2 = 2.5
Step 2: Area ratio = k² = (5/2)² = 25/4
Step 3: Area of larger = 36 × (25/4) = 36 × 6.25 = 225 cm²
The larger trapezoid has an area of 225 cm².

lessons.tip: When writing a similarity statement, order matters just like in congruence statements. If ABCD ~ EFGH, then A corresponds to E, B to F, and so on. Always list the vertices in corresponding order to avoid confusion when setting up proportions.

quiz.q: Two similar rectangles have a scale factor of 2:7. What is the ratio of their areas?
quiz.explanation: The ratio of areas of similar figures equals the square of the scale factor: (2/7)² = 4/49, so the area ratio is 4:49.

quiz.q: For two polygons to be similar, which must be true?
options: All corresponding angles are congruent only
All corresponding sides are proportional only
Both: all corresponding angles are congruent AND all corresponding sides are proportional
The polygons have the same perimeter
quiz.explanation: Similarity requires both conditions: congruent corresponding angles AND proportional corresponding sides. Either condition alone is not sufficient.

quiz.q: If ΔABC ~ ΔDEF with a scale factor of 3:4, and AB = 9, what is DE?
quiz.explanation: Scale factor DE/AB = 4/3. So DE = AB × (4/3) = 9 × (4/3) = 12.

lessons.title: Similar Triangles
lessons.description: Learn AA, SAS, and SSS similarity criteria.
lessons.formula:
Triangle Similarity Criteria:
• AA (Angle-Angle): If 2 angles of one Δ ≡ 2 angles of another Δ → ~
• SSS (Side-Side-Side): If all 3 sides of one Δ are proportional to another → ~
• SAS (Side-Angle-Side): If 2 sides are proportional AND the included angle is ≡ → ~

Proportionality of sides:
AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF = k (scale factor)

Perimeter ratio = k
Area ratio = k²
lessons.content:
Triangles can be proven similar using three criteria, which parallel (but are slightly different from) the congruence postulates. The AA (Angle-Angle) Similarity Postulate is the most commonly used: if two angles of one triangle are congruent to two angles of another triangle, the triangles are similar. This works because if two angles are the same, the third must also be the same (since angles sum to 180°), so all three angles match.

The SSS Similarity Theorem states that if all three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional (with the same scale factor), the triangles are similar. The SAS Similarity Theorem requires that two pairs of sides are proportional and the included angles are congruent. Note the key difference from congruence: for similarity, sides must be proportional (same ratio) rather than congruent (equal length).

Similar triangles are especially powerful because of their relationship to real-world measurement. If you can identify two similar triangles, you can set up proportions to find unknown distances that are difficult to measure directly. This is the basis of indirect measurement, used in surveying, astronomy, and navigation. Common applications include finding the height of a tree using its shadow and similar right triangles, or calculating distances across rivers.
steps: Identify the two triangles and determine which similarity criterion might apply
For AA: find two pairs of congruent angles (vertical, corresponding, alternate interior, etc.)
For SSS: check if all three side ratios are equal
For SAS: check if two side ratios are equal AND the included angles are congruent
Once similarity is established, set up proportions to find unknown side lengths
Solve the proportion by cross-multiplying

examples.title: Example 1: Proving Similarity with AA
examples.text:
In ΔABC and ΔDEF: ∠A ≡ ∠D = 50°, ∠B ≡ ∠E = 70°.

Step 1: Two pairs of angles are congruent: ∠A ≡ ∠D and ∠B ≡ ∠E
Step 2: By the AA Similarity Postulate, ΔABC ~ ΔDEF
Step 3: The third angles are also congruent: ∠C = 180° – 50° – 70° = 60° = ∠F
All three angles match, confirming the similarity.

examples.title: Example 2: Finding a Missing Side Using Similarity
examples.text:
ΔPQR ~ ΔSTU. PQ = 6, QR = 8, ST = 15, and TU = x. Find x.

Step 1: Since the triangles are similar, PQ/ST = QR/TU
Step 2: 6/15 = 8/x
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 6x = 15 × 8 = 120
Step 4: x = 120/6 = 20
TU = 20. The scale factor is 15/6 = 5/2 = 2.5.

lessons.tip: AA is the easiest and most commonly used similarity criterion because you only need to find two congruent angles. Look for shared angles, vertical angles, or angles formed by parallel lines (corresponding and alternate interior) to quickly identify AA similarity.

quiz.q: Which similarity criterion requires two sides to be proportional and the included angle to be congruent?
quiz.explanation: SAS Similarity requires two pairs of proportional sides and the included angle to be congruent, mirroring the SAS congruence pattern but with proportions instead of equality.

quiz.q: ΔABC and ΔDEF have ∠A ≡ ∠D and ∠C ≡ ∠F. Which criterion proves similarity?
quiz.explanation: Two pairs of congruent angles are sufficient for AA Similarity. The third angles are automatically congruent since they complete the 180° sum.

quiz.q: In similar triangles ΔXYZ ~ ΔABC, if XY = 4, AB = 12, and YZ = 6, what is BC?
quiz.explanation: The scale factor is AB/XY = 12/4 = 3. So BC = YZ × 3 = 6 × 3 = 18.

lessons.title: Applications of Similarity
lessons.description: Apply similarity to solve real-world problems.
lessons.formula:
Indirect Measurement (Shadow Method):
(Object height) / (Shadow length) = (Reference height) / (Reference shadow length)
h₁/s₁ = h₂/s₂

Scale Models:
Scale ratio = model dimension / actual dimension
Actual size = model size ÷ scale ratio

Map Scale:
Map distance = Actual distance × map scale
Example: 1 inch = 100 miles means scale = 1/100

Area of actual = Area of model × (scale factor)²
lessons.content:
Similar triangles have powerful real-world applications, primarily through a technique called indirect measurement. When you cannot directly measure a height or distance (like a tall building or a river crossing), you can set up similar triangles to calculate it from measurable quantities. The most common method is the shadow method: on a sunny day, a person and a tall object both cast shadows that form similar right triangles with the ground, since the sun's rays are essentially parallel.

Scale models and drawings are another major application of similarity. Architects create scale models of buildings, cartographers produce maps at reduced scales, and engineers build prototype models. If a model has a scale of 1:50, every measurement on the model is 1/50th of the actual measurement. To convert between model and actual dimensions, simply multiply or divide by the scale factor. Remember that areas scale by the square of the linear scale factor: a 1:50 scale model has an area ratio of 1:2500.

Another practical application is using similar triangles in photography and vision. The image formed on a camera sensor (or your retina) is a scaled version of the actual scene, creating similar triangles between the object, lens, and image plane. Understanding these proportions helps in calculating focal lengths, object distances, and magnification. Whether measuring a tree's height with a shadow, reading a map, or designing a building, similarity principles are at work.
steps: Identify the real-world situation that involves similar triangles (shadows, mirrors, scale drawings)
Draw a diagram showing the two similar triangles with all known measurements labeled
Set up a proportion using corresponding sides of the similar triangles
Solve the proportion using cross-multiplication to find the unknown value
For scale models, multiply or divide by the scale factor to convert between actual and model sizes
Verify your answer by checking that the proportion holds for all corresponding side pairs

examples.title: Example 1: Finding the Height of a Building
examples.text:
A 5-foot-tall person casts a shadow 8 feet long. At the same time, a nearby building casts a shadow 96 feet long. How tall is the building?

Step 1: The person and building form similar right triangles with their shadows.
Step 2: Set up proportion: 5/8 = h/96
Step 3: Cross-multiply: 8h = 5 × 96 = 480
Step 4: h = 480/8 = 60 feet
The building is 60 feet tall.

examples.title: Example 2: Working with a Scale Drawing
examples.text:
A scale drawing of a room uses 1 inch = 4 feet. The drawing shows a room that is 3.5 inches wide and 5 inches long. What are the actual dimensions? What is the actual area?

Step 1: Actual width = 3.5 × 4 = 14 feet
Step 2: Actual length = 5 × 4 = 20 feet
Step 3: Actual area = 14 × 20 = 280 square feet
Or using area scaling: Drawing area = 3.5 × 5 = 17.5 sq in
Scale factor = 4, so area scale = 16
Actual area = 17.5 × 16 = 280 sq ft ✓

lessons.tip: The shadow method works best when both shadows are measured at the same time of day (so the sun angle is the same for both). If you don't have a shadow available, you can also use a mirror on the ground and the reflection principle — the triangles formed by the eye, mirror, and objects are similar by AA (shared angle at the mirror and right angles).

quiz.q: A 6-foot pole casts a 10-foot shadow. A nearby tree casts a 45-foot shadow. How tall is the tree?
quiz.explanation: Set up the proportion: 6/10 = h/45. Cross-multiply: 10h = 270, so h = 27 feet.

quiz.q: A map has a scale of 1 cm = 5 km. Two cities are 8.5 cm apart on the map. What is the actual distance?
quiz.explanation: Actual distance = 8.5 cm × 5 km/cm = 42.5 km.

quiz.q: A scale model car is built at a scale of 1:24. If the model is 18 cm long, what is the actual car's length?
quiz.explanation: Actual length = model length × scale factor = 18 × 24 = 432 cm (4.32 meters).

lessons.title: Pythagorean Theorem
lessons.description: Apply a² + b² = c² to right triangles.
lessons.formula:
Pythagorean Theorem:
a² + b² = c²
where a and b are legs, c is the hypotenuse

Solving for a leg:
a² = c² – b²

Converse of the Pythagorean Theorem:
If a² + b² = c² → the triangle is right
If a² + b² > c² → the triangle is acute
If a² + b² < c² → the triangle is obtuse

Common Pythagorean Triples:
(3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25)
lessons.content:
The Pythagorean Theorem is one of the most famous and useful results in all of mathematics. It states that in a right triangle, the square of the length of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the lengths of the two legs. In formula form: a² + b² = c², where c represents the hypotenuse and a, b represent the legs. Named after the ancient Greek mathematician Pythagoras, this theorem applies to every right triangle without exception.

The converse of the Pythagorean Theorem is equally useful: if the three sides of a triangle satisfy a² + b² = c², then the triangle is a right triangle. This lets you test whether a triangle is right-angled by checking its side lengths. The converse also leads to triangle classification tests: if a² + b² > c², the triangle is acute (all angles less than 90°); if a² + b² < c², the triangle is obtuse (one angle greater than 90°).

Pythagorean triples are sets of three positive integers that satisfy the theorem. The most common are (3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (8, 15, 17), and (7, 24, 25). Any multiple of a Pythagorean triple is also a triple: (6, 8, 10), (9, 12, 15), (10, 24, 26), etc. Recognizing these triples lets you quickly identify right triangles and solve problems without a calculator. The theorem has applications in construction, navigation, physics, computer graphics, and countless other fields.
steps: Identify the right triangle and label the hypotenuse (longest side, opposite the right angle)
Label the two legs as a and b, and the hypotenuse as c
Substitute the known values into a² + b² = c²
If finding the hypotenuse: compute a² + b², then take the square root
If finding a leg: rearrange to a² = c² – b², then take the square root
For the converse: compute a² + b² and c², then compare to classify the triangle

examples.title: Example 1: Finding the Hypotenuse
examples.text:
A right triangle has legs measuring 9 cm and 12 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

Step 1: a = 9, b = 12, c = ?
Step 2: a² + b² = c²
Step 3: 9² + 12² = c²
Step 4: 81 + 144 = c²
Step 5: c² = 225
Step 6: c = √225 = 15 cm
Note: (9, 12, 15) is a multiple of the (3, 4, 5) triple.

examples.title: Example 2: Using the Converse to Classify a Triangle
examples.text:
A triangle has sides 4, 6, and 7. Is it acute, right, or obtuse?

Step 1: The longest side is 7, so check: 4² + 6² compared to 7²
Step 2: 4² + 6² = 16 + 36 = 52
Step 3: 7² = 49
Step 4: Since 52 > 49 (a² + b² > c²), the triangle is acute.
All three angles are less than 90°.

lessons.tip: Memorize the first few Pythagorean triples: (3,4,5), (5,12,13), (8,15,17), (7,24,25). When you see side lengths that are multiples of these (like 6,8,10 or 15,20,25), you can instantly identify them as right triangles without doing any calculations.

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs of 5 cm and 12 cm. What is the length of the hypotenuse?
quiz.explanation: 5² + 12² = 25 + 144 = 169 = 13². The hypotenuse is 13 cm. This is the classic (5, 12, 13) triple.

quiz.q: A triangle has sides 5, 7, and 9. Using the converse, this triangle is:
quiz.explanation: 5² + 7² = 25 + 49 = 74, and 9² = 81. Since 74 < 81, a² + b² < c², so the triangle is obtuse.

quiz.q: Which set of numbers is a Pythagorean triple?
quiz.explanation: 6² + 8² = 36 + 64 = 100 = 10². This is a multiple of (3, 4, 5). The other sets do not satisfy a² + b² = c².

lessons.title: Special Right Triangles
lessons.description: Solve problems with 45-45-90 and 30-60-90 triangles.
lessons.formula:
45°-45°-90° Triangle (Isosceles Right Triangle):
Legs: a, a
Hypotenuse: a√2
Ratio of sides: 1 : 1 : √2

30°-60°-90° Triangle:
Short leg (opposite 30°): a
Long leg (opposite 60°): a√3
Hypotenuse: 2a
Ratio of sides: 1 : √3 : 2

Common values:
• (1, 1, √2), (2, 2, 2√2), (5, 5, 5√2)
• (1, √3, 2), (2, 2√3, 4), (3, 3√3, 6)
lessons.content:
45-45-90 triangles and 30-60-90 triangles are two special types of right triangles whose side lengths follow predictable patterns. These patterns let you find side lengths quickly without using the full Pythagorean Theorem. The 45-45-90 triangle is an isosceles right triangle — both legs are equal, and the hypotenuse is the leg length multiplied by √2. For example, if each leg is 5, the hypotenuse is 5√2.

The 30-60-90 triangle has three distinct side lengths following the ratio 1 : √3 : 2. The shortest side is opposite the 30° angle, the medium side (short leg × √3) is opposite the 60° angle, and the hypotenuse (short leg × 2) is opposite the 90° angle. For example, if the short leg is 7, the long leg is 7√3 and the hypotenuse is 14. If you know the hypotenuse, the short leg is half of it, and the long leg is the short leg times √3.

These special triangles appear frequently in geometry problems, especially those involving squares (diagonals create 45-45-90 triangles), equilateral triangles (altitudes create 30-60-90 triangles), and regular hexagons. Recognizing these patterns saves significant time on tests and in applications. Many standardized test problems are specifically designed so that special right triangle shortcuts apply, giving you a fast path to the answer.
steps: Determine which type of special right triangle you have based on the given angle measures
For 45-45-90: if given a leg, multiply by √2 for the hypotenuse; if given the hypotenuse, divide by √2 for each leg
For 30-60-90: identify the short leg (opposite 30°) as your starting value a
Long leg = a√3, hypotenuse = 2a
If given the hypotenuse in a 30-60-90 triangle, divide by 2 to find the short leg, then multiply by √3 for the long leg
Rationalize denominators if needed (multiply numerator and denominator by √2 or √3)

examples.title: Example 1: 45-45-90 Triangle Problem
examples.text:
The diagonal of a square measures 12√2 cm. Find the side length of the square.

Step 1: The diagonal of a square creates two 45-45-90 triangles.
Step 2: In a 45-45-90 triangle, hypotenuse = leg × √2.
Step 3: 12√2 = leg × √2
Step 4: leg = 12√2 / √2 = 12 cm
The side of the square is 12 cm.

examples.title: Example 2: 30-60-90 Triangle Problem
examples.text:
An equilateral triangle has sides of 10 cm. Find the length of its altitude.

Step 1: The altitude of an equilateral triangle creates two 30-60-90 triangles.
Step 2: The hypotenuse of each 30-60-90 triangle is 10 (side of the equilateral triangle).
Step 3: Short leg (half the base) = 10/2 = 5 cm
Step 4: Long leg (altitude) = 5√3 cm
The altitude is 5√3 cm (approximately 8.66 cm).

lessons.tip: For 30-60-90 triangles, memorize the pattern as "short, short×√3, short×2." For 45-45-90 triangles, remember "leg, leg, leg×√2." When you see √2 or √3 in a side length, it is almost always a clue that a special right triangle is involved.

quiz.q: In a 45-45-90 triangle, if a leg is 8 cm, what is the hypotenuse?
quiz.explanation: In a 45-45-90 triangle, the hypotenuse = leg × √2 = 8√2 cm.

quiz.q: In a 30-60-90 triangle, the hypotenuse is 14. What is the length of the side opposite 60°?
quiz.explanation: Short leg = 14/2 = 7. Long leg (opposite 60°) = 7√3.

quiz.q: The diagonal of a square is 6√2. What is the perimeter of the square?
quiz.explanation: Side = diagonal/√2 = 6√2/√2 = 6. Perimeter = 4 × 6 = 24.

lessons.title: Introduction to Trigonometry
lessons.description: Learn the basic trigonometric ratios: sine, cosine, tangent.
lessons.formula:
SOH-CAH-TOA (for acute angles in right triangles):

sin(θ) = Opposite / Hypotenuse
cos(θ) = Adjacent / Hypotenuse
tan(θ) = Opposite / Adjacent

Inverse functions to find angles:
θ = arcsin(O/H) = sin⁻¹(O/H)
θ = arccos(A/H) = cos⁻¹(A/H)
θ = arctan(O/A) = tan⁻¹(O/A)

Common trig values:
sin(30°) = 1/2, cos(30°) = √3/2, tan(30°) = 1/√3
sin(45°) = √2/2, cos(45°) = √2/2, tan(45°) = 1
sin(60°) = √3/2, cos(60°) = 1/2, tan(60°) = √3
lessons.content:
Trigonometry is the branch of mathematics that studies the relationships between angles and sides of triangles. In a right triangle, the three primary trigonometric ratios — sine, cosine, and tangent — relate an acute angle to the lengths of the triangle's sides. These ratios are constant for a given angle, regardless of the triangle's size. The mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA helps you remember: Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent/Hypotenuse, Tangent = Opposite/Adjacent.

To use these ratios, you must correctly identify which side is opposite the angle (the side across from the angle), which side is adjacent (the side next to the angle that is not the hypotenuse), and which side is the hypotenuse (always opposite the right angle, the longest side). For a given angle θ in a right triangle, the opposite and adjacent sides change depending on which acute angle you choose, but the hypotenuse is always the same. This distinction is critical and a common source of error.

Trigonometric ratios are used in two main ways. First, if you know an angle, you can find a ratio using a calculator (in degree mode). Second, if you know two sides of a right triangle, you can find an angle using the inverse trigonometric functions (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, tan⁻¹). Applications include finding heights of buildings, calculating distances in navigation, analyzing forces in physics, and designing structures in engineering. The common angle values for 30°, 45°, and 60° connect directly to the special right triangles from the previous lesson.
steps: Label the right triangle: mark the right angle, identify the hypotenuse (always longest, opposite 90°)
Identify the angle of interest (θ) and label the opposite side and adjacent side relative to it
Decide which trig ratio to use based on the sides you know and the side you need to find
Set up the equation using SOH, CAH, or TOA
Solve for the unknown side or angle
If finding an angle, use the inverse function (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, or tan⁻¹) and ensure your calculator is in degree mode

examples.title: Example 1: Finding a Side Using Sine
examples.text:
In right ΔABC, ∠A = 35°, the hypotenuse BC = 12 cm. Find the length of the opposite side AB.

Step 1: We know the angle (35°) and the hypotenuse (12). We need the opposite side.
Step 2: Use sine: sin(35°) = opposite/hypotenuse = AB/12
Step 3: AB = 12 × sin(35°) = 12 × 0.5736 ≈ 6.88 cm
The side AB is approximately 6.88 cm.

examples.title: Example 2: Finding an Angle Using Inverse Tangent
examples.text:
A ramp rises 3 feet over a horizontal distance of 10 feet. What angle does the ramp make with the ground?

Step 1: The opposite side = 3 ft (rise), adjacent side = 10 ft (run).
Step 2: Use tangent: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent = 3/10 = 0.3
Step 3: θ = tan⁻¹(0.3) ≈ 16.7°
The ramp makes an angle of approximately 16.7° with the ground.

lessons.tip: The most common mistake in trigonometry is confusing the opposite and adjacent sides. Remember: "opposite" means across from the angle you're working with, and "adjacent" means next to it (but never the hypotenuse). Before setting up any ratio, take two seconds to point at the angle, trace to the opposite side, and trace to the adjacent side.

quiz.q: In a right triangle, which ratio does SOH-CAH-TOA tell you for sine?
quiz.explanation: SOH stands for Sine = Opposite/Hypotenuse. The opposite side is across from the angle of interest, and the hypotenuse is always the longest side.

quiz.q: In a right triangle, cos(θ) = 0.6 and the hypotenuse is 10. What is the length of the adjacent side?
quiz.explanation: cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse, so 0.6 = adjacent/10. Therefore, adjacent = 10 × 0.6 = 6.

quiz.q: A right triangle has legs of 3 and 4. What is tan(θ) where θ is the angle opposite the side of length 3?
quiz.explanation: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent = 3/4. The opposite side is 3 and the adjacent side is 4 (relative to angle θ).

lessons.title: Sine
lessons.description: Understand and apply the sine ratio.
lessons.formula:
sin(θ) = opposite / hypotenuse

opposite = sin(θ) × hypotenuse

hypotenuse = opposite / sin(θ)
lessons.content:
The sine ratio is one of the three primary trigonometric functions used with right triangles. For any acute angle θ in a right triangle, sine is defined as the ratio of the length of the side opposite the angle to the length of the hypotenuse (the longest side, opposite the right angle). The mnemonic SOH-CAH-TOA helps you remember: Sine = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse.

To find a missing side using sine, first identify the reference angle and label the sides as opposite, adjacent, and hypotenuse. Then set up the proportion sin(θ) = opposite / hypotenuse and solve for the unknown using cross-multiplication. Always use a calculator in degree mode for degree measures or radian mode for radian measures.

Sine values range from 0 to 1 for angles between 0° and 90°. Common reference values include sin(30°) = 1/2, sin(45°) = √2/2 ≈ 0.707, and sin(60°) = √3/2 ≈ 0.866. These exact values appear frequently on standardized tests and in proofs.
steps: Identify the right triangle and locate the reference angle θ.
Label the three sides: opposite (across from θ), adjacent (next to θ), and hypotenuse (longest side).
Write the sine ratio: sin(θ) = opposite / hypotenuse.
Substitute the known values into the equation.
Solve for the unknown side by cross-multiplying or dividing.
Round your answer to the desired precision and include units.

examples.title: Finding the Opposite Side
examples.text:
A ladder leans against a wall at a 65° angle with the ground. The ladder is 10 ft long (hypotenuse). Find the height the ladder reaches on the wall.

sin(65°) = opposite / 10
opposite = 10 × sin(65°) = 10 × 0.9063 ≈ 9.06 ft

examples.title: Finding the Hypotenuse
examples.text:
A right triangle has an angle of 40° and the side opposite that angle is 7 cm. Find the hypotenuse.

sin(40°) = 7 / hypotenuse
hypotenuse = 7 / sin(40°) = 7 / 0.6428 ≈ 10.89 cm

lessons.tip: Remember SOH from SOH-CAH-TOA: Sine = Opposite over Hypotenuse. When solving word problems involving heights or angles of elevation/depression, draw a diagram first and label all known sides before setting up your sine equation.

quiz.q: In a right triangle with angle θ = 30° and hypotenuse = 12, what is the length of the opposite side?
Which side does the sine ratio use in the numerator?
quiz.explanation: Sine = Opposite / Hypotenuse. The numerator is the side opposite the reference angle.

quiz.q: If sin(θ) = 3/5 and the hypotenuse is 20, what is the opposite side?

lessons.title: Cosine
lessons.description: Understand and apply the cosine ratio.
lessons.formula:
cos(θ) = adjacent / hypotenuse

adjacent = cos(θ) × hypotenuse

hypotenuse = adjacent / cos(θ)
lessons.content:
The cosine ratio is the second of the three primary trigonometric functions for right triangles. For an acute angle θ, cosine equals the ratio of the length of the adjacent side (the leg next to θ that is not the hypotenuse) to the length of the hypotenuse. In the SOH-CAH-TOA mnemonic, CAH stands for Cosine = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse.

Cosine and sine are complementary functions: for any angle θ, cos(θ) = sin(90° − θ). This means the cosine of one acute angle in a right triangle equals the sine of the other acute angle. Common reference values include cos(30°) = √3/2 ≈ 0.866, cos(45°) = √2/2 ≈ 0.707, and cos(60°) = 1/2.

To use cosine in problems, identify the reference angle and the adjacent side carefully. In real-world applications, cosine frequently appears when you need to find horizontal distances (shadows, ground distances) when the hypotenuse and an angle are known.
steps: Identify the reference angle θ in the right triangle.
Label the adjacent side (the leg touching θ that is not the hypotenuse) and the hypotenuse.
Write the cosine ratio: cos(θ) = adjacent / hypotenuse.
Substitute the known values into the equation.
Cross-multiply or rearrange to isolate the unknown side.
Check your answer is reasonable (e.g., the adjacent side should be shorter than the hypotenuse).

examples.title: Finding the Adjacent Side
examples.text:
A ramp makes a 25° angle with the ground. The ramp is 15 ft long. How far along the ground does the ramp reach?

cos(25°) = adjacent / 15
adjacent = 15 × cos(25°) = 15 × 0.9063 ≈ 13.59 ft

examples.title: Finding the Hypotenuse with Cosine
examples.text:
In a right triangle, angle θ = 55° and the adjacent side is 9 m. Find the hypotenuse.

cos(55°) = 9 / hypotenuse
hypotenuse = 9 / cos(55°) = 9 / 0.5736 ≈ 15.69 m

lessons.tip: CAH from SOH-CAH-TOA: Cosine = Adjacent over Hypotenuse. A quick check: since the adjacent side is always shorter than the hypotenuse, cos(θ) should always be less than 1 for acute angles.

quiz.q: In a right triangle with angle θ = 60° and hypotenuse = 10, what is the adjacent side?
If cos(θ) = 4/5 and the adjacent side is 20, what is the hypotenuse?
Which identity relates sine and cosine for complementary angles?
quiz.explanation: Sine and cosine are co-functions: sin(θ) = cos(90° − θ). The sine of an angle equals the cosine of its complement.

lessons.title: Tangent
lessons.description: Understand and apply the tangent ratio.
lessons.formula:
tan(θ) = opposite / adjacent

opposite = tan(θ) × adjacent

adjacent = opposite / tan(θ)
lessons.content:
The tangent ratio is the third primary trigonometric function for right triangles. For an acute angle θ, tangent equals the ratio of the opposite side to the adjacent side. In SOH-CAH-TOA, TOA stands for Tangent = Opposite ÷ Adjacent. Unlike sine and cosine, tangent does not involve the hypotenuse at all.

Tangent can also be expressed as sin(θ)/cos(θ), which reveals an important property: tan(90°) is undefined because cos(90°) = 0, causing division by zero. Common reference values include tan(30°) = √3/3 ≈ 0.577, tan(45°) = 1, and tan(60°) = √3 ≈ 1.732.

In real-world contexts, tangent is ideal for problems involving slopes, grades of roads, and heights of objects when the ground distance is known. When the angle approaches 90°, the tangent grows without bound, which is why a perfectly vertical slope is described as having an undefined grade.
steps: Identify the reference angle θ in the right triangle.
Label the opposite side (across from θ) and the adjacent side (next to θ, not the hypotenuse).
Write the tangent ratio: tan(θ) = opposite / adjacent.
Substitute the known values into the equation.
Solve for the unknown by multiplying or dividing as needed.
Verify your answer makes sense geometrically (e.g., opposite can be larger than adjacent).

examples.title: Finding the Opposite Side
examples.text:
A person stands 50 m from the base of a building. The angle of elevation to the top is 32°. Find the building's height.

tan(32°) = height / 50
height = 50 × tan(32°) = 50 × 0.6249 ≈ 31.2 m

examples.title: Finding the Adjacent Side
examples.text:
A tree casts a shadow. The angle of elevation of the sun is 50°, and the tree is 18 ft tall. Find the shadow length.

tan(50°) = 18 / shadow
shadow = 18 / tan(50°) = 18 / 1.1918 ≈ 15.1 ft

lessons.tip: TOA from SOH-CAH-TOA: Tangent = Opposite over Adjacent. Tangent is especially useful for finding heights and distances on level ground. Note that tan(45°) = 1, which means at 45° the opposite and adjacent sides are equal — a perfect isosceles right triangle.

quiz.q: In a right triangle with angle θ = 45° and adjacent side = 8, what is the opposite side?
quiz.explanation: tan(45°) = 1, so opposite = adjacent × 1 = 8.

quiz.q: What is tan(60°) equal to?
Why is tan(90°) undefined?
options: The adjacent side is zero, causing division by zero
90° is not a valid angle in trigonometry
quiz.explanation: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent. At 90°, the adjacent side has length 0, so we divide by zero, which is undefined.

lessons.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
lessons.description: Use inverse trig to find unknown angles.
lessons.formula:
θ = sin⁻¹(opposite / hypotenuse)
θ = cos⁻¹(adjacent / hypotenuse)
θ = tan⁻¹(opposite / adjacent)

Domain of sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹: [−1, 1]
Range of sin⁻¹: [−90°, 90°]
Range of cos⁻¹: [0°, 180°]
Range of tan⁻¹: [−90°, 90°]
lessons.content:
Inverse trigonometric functions (also called arcsine, arccosine, and arctangent) do the reverse of the regular trig functions: instead of taking an angle and returning a ratio, they take a ratio and return the angle. If sin(θ) = 0.5, then θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°. These are the tools you use when you know the side lengths of a right triangle and need to find an unknown angle.

To use an inverse trig function on a calculator, you typically press the 2nd or Shift key followed by the sin, cos, or tan button. Always make sure your calculator is in the correct angle mode (degrees or radians). The input to sin⁻¹ and cos⁻¹ must be between −1 and 1, and the input to tan⁻¹ can be any real number.

Inverse trig functions are essential in navigation, engineering, and physics. For example, determining the launch angle of a projectile or the angle at which a roof is inclined both require inverse trigonometry. Remember: the output angle from sin⁻¹ is always in the range [−90°, 90°], from cos⁻¹ is in [0°, 180°], and from tan⁻¹ is in (−90°, 90°).
steps: Identify which sides of the right triangle are known.
Decide which trig ratio to use based on the two known sides (opposite/hypotenuse → sin⁻¹, adjacent/hypotenuse → cos⁻¹, opposite/adjacent → tan⁻¹).
Calculate the ratio of the two known sides.
Apply the appropriate inverse function: θ = sin⁻¹(ratio), θ = cos⁻¹(ratio), or θ = tan⁻¹(ratio).
Round the angle to the nearest tenth of a degree if needed.
Verify by substituting the angle back into the original trig function to confirm it gives the correct ratio.

examples.title: Finding an Angle Using sin⁻¹
examples.text:
A right triangle has opposite side = 5 and hypotenuse = 10. Find angle θ.

sin(θ) = 5/10 = 0.5
θ = sin⁻¹(0.5) = 30°

examples.title: Finding an Angle Using tan⁻¹
examples.text:
A person stands 30 m from a flagpole and sees the top at an angle. The flagpole is 20 m tall. Find the angle of elevation.

tan(θ) = 20/30 = 0.6667
θ = tan⁻¹(0.6667) ≈ 33.7°

lessons.tip: Think of inverse trig functions as 'undoing' regular trig. If you set up sin(θ) = ratio, then press 2nd+sin on your calculator and enter the ratio to get θ. Always double-check: does the angle make sense given the side lengths?

quiz.q: If opposite = 7 and hypotenuse = 14, what is angle θ using the inverse sine function?
sin⁻¹(sin(55°)) equals what?
quiz.explanation: sin⁻¹ and sin are inverse functions, so sin⁻¹(sin(55°)) = 55°.

quiz.q: Which inverse function should you use when you know the opposite and adjacent sides?
quiz.explanation: tan(θ) = opposite/adjacent, so θ = tan⁻¹(opposite/adjacent).

lessons.title: Law of Sines
lessons.description: Apply the Law of Sines to any triangle (HONORS).
lessons.formula:
a / sin(A) = b / sin(B) = c / sin(C)

or equivalently:
sin(A) / a = sin(B) / b = sin(C) / c

Used when you know: AAS, ASA, or SSA (ambiguous case)
lessons.content:
The Law of Sines extends trigonometry beyond right triangles to any triangle. It states that the ratio of a side length to the sine of its opposite angle is constant: a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C). This law works for all triangles — acute, obtuse, and right — and is especially useful when you know two angles and one side (ASA or AAS) or two sides and an angle opposite one of them (SSA).

The ambiguous case (SSA condition) occurs when you know two sides and an angle that is not included between them. Depending on the measurements, there can be 0, 1, or 2 possible triangles. To resolve the ambiguous case: (1) find the height h = b·sin(A); (2) if side a < h, no triangle exists; (3) if a = h, one right triangle; (4) if h < a < b, two triangles; (5) if a ≥ b, one triangle.

When applying the Law of Sines, always find the largest angle first when possible, since the largest angle is always opposite the longest side and must be obtuse if it exceeds 90°. This prevents the ambiguity issue in many cases.
steps: Identify the known values: sides and angles. Label the triangle consistently (side a opposite angle A, etc.).
Verify the Law of Sines applies (ASA, AAS, or SSA configuration).
Write the proportion: a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C).
Substitute the known values and set up an equation to find the unknown.
Solve for the unknown angle using an inverse sine function, or for a side using cross-multiplication.
If SSA (ambiguous case), check for 0, 1, or 2 solutions using the height test.

examples.title: Finding a Side (AAS)
examples.text:
In triangle ABC, angle A = 42°, angle B = 73°, and side a = 15. Find side b.

a/sin(A) = b/sin(B)
15/sin(42°) = b/sin(73°)
b = 15 × sin(73°) / sin(42°) = 15 × 0.9563 / 0.6691 ≈ 21.4

examples.title: Finding an Angle (SSA — check for ambiguity)
examples.text:
In triangle ABC, side a = 10, side b = 15, angle A = 35°. Find angle B.

sin(B)/b = sin(A)/a
sin(B) = 15 × sin(35°) / 10 = 15 × 0.5736 / 10 = 0.8604
B = sin⁻¹(0.8604) ≈ 59.4°

Check: B' = 180° − 59.4° = 120.6°. Since A + B' = 35° + 120.6° = 155.6° < 180°, TWO triangles exist.

lessons.tip: The Law of Sines is ideal for non-right triangles when you have AAS or ASA. For the ambiguous SSA case, always draw both possible triangles and compute angles to see if the second solution is valid (sum of angles must be less than 180°).

quiz.q: The Law of Sines states that a/sin(A) equals what?
quiz.explanation: The Law of Sines: a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C).

quiz.q: In the ambiguous case (SSA), how many triangles are possible when h < a < b?
quiz.explanation: When the given side a is between the height h and side b, two distinct triangles can be formed.

quiz.q: Which configurations allow direct use of the Law of Sines?
quiz.explanation: The Law of Sines requires knowing at least one angle-side opposite pair, which ASA and AAS provide directly.

lessons.title: Law of Cosines
lessons.description: Apply the Law of Cosines to any triangle (HONORS).
lessons.formula:
c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos(C)

Solving for an angle:
cos(C) = (a² + b² − c²) / (2ab)

When C = 90°: c² = a² + b² (reduces to Pythagorean theorem)
lessons.content:
The Law of Cosines generalizes the Pythagorean theorem to all triangles. For any triangle with sides a, b, c and angle C opposite side c: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos(C). When C = 90°, cos(C) = 0 and the formula reduces to the familiar c² = a² + b². This law is the go-to tool when the Law of Sines cannot be applied directly.

Use the Law of Cosines when you know SAS (two sides and the included angle) to find the third side, or when you know SSS (all three sides) to find any angle. Unlike the Law of Sines, the Law of Cosines has no ambiguous case — each set of given values produces exactly one solution, making it more reliable in many situations.

The rearranged form cos(C) = (a² + b² − c²)/(2ab) is especially useful for finding angles when all three sides are known (SSS). In real-world applications, the Law of Cosines is used in surveying, GPS calculations, physics (vector addition), and computer graphics.
steps: Identify the known values and label the triangle (side c opposite angle C, etc.).
Verify you have SAS (find a side) or SSS (find an angle).
Write the Law of Cosines: c² = a² + b² − 2ab·cos(C).
Substitute known values into the formula.
If finding a side: compute the right side and take the square root. If finding an angle: rearrange to cos(C) = (a²+b²−c²)/(2ab), then apply cos⁻¹.
Find the remaining angle(s) using the Law of Sines or sum of angles (180°).
lessons.tip: Use Law of Cosines for SAS and SSS; use Law of Sines for ASA and AAS. If you have SSA (ambiguous case), try Law of Sines first, but switch to Law of Cosines if ambiguity is a problem. The Law of Cosines always gives a unique answer.

quiz.q: The Law of Cosines reduces to the Pythagorean theorem when the angle is:
quiz.explanation: When C = 90°, cos(90°) = 0, so c² = a² + b² − 0 = a² + b².

quiz.q: Given sides a = 5, b = 7, c = 9, which formula finds angle C?
What is a key advantage of the Law of Cosines over the Law of Sines?
options: It only works for acute triangles
quiz.explanation: The Law of Cosines has no ambiguous case — each input produces exactly one valid triangle.

lessons.title: Properties of Quadrilaterals Overview
lessons.description: Learn about all types of quadrilaterals — parallelograms, rectangles, rhombuses, squares, trapezoids, and kites. Compare their sides, angles, and diagonals!
lessons.formula:
Quadrilateral Properties Comparison:

┌─────────────┬──────────┬────────┬──────────┬──────────────┐
│  Shape       │  Sides   │ Angles │ Diagonals │  Special     │
├─────────────┼──────────┼────────┼──────────┼──────────────┤
│ Parallelogram│ 2 pairs ║│ Opp ≅  │ Bisect   │ Opp sides ≅  │
│ Rectangle   │ 2 pairs ║│ All 90° │ Bisect,≅ │ Opp sides ≅  │
│ Rhombus     │ All ≅    │ Opp ≅  │ ⊥ Bisect │ Diags. ⊥     │
│ Square      │ All ≅    │ All 90° │ ⊥,≅,Bisect│ ALL props!  │
│ Trapezoid   │ 1 pair ║ │ Varies  │ Varies   │ Isosceles: ≅ │
│ Kite        │ 2 pairs ≅│ Varies  │ 1 ⊥ bisect│ Adj. ≅ sides│
└─────────────┴──────────┴────────┴──────────┴──────────────┘

║ = parallel, ≅ = congruent, ⊥ = perpendicular
lessons.content:
A quadrilateral is any four-sided polygon. But not all quadrilaterals are created equal! Different types have special properties related to their sides, angles, and diagonals. Understanding these properties helps you classify shapes, solve geometry problems, and prove theorems.

Parallelograms have two pairs of parallel sides. The opposite sides are congruent and parallel, opposite angles are congruent, and the diagonals bisect each other. Rectangles, rhombuses, and squares are all special types of parallelograms. A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. A rhombus is a parallelogram with four congruent sides. A square is BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus — it has all the properties!

Trapezoids have exactly one pair of parallel sides (called bases). An isosceles trapezoid has congruent legs (non-parallel sides) and congruent base angles. Kites have two pairs of adjacent congruent sides, with one diagonal that is the perpendicular bisector of the other.
steps: Count the sides: a quadrilateral always has 4 sides
Check for parallel sides: 2 pairs = parallelogram family, 1 pair = trapezoid, 0 = irregular
If parallelogram: check angles (all 90° = rectangle) and sides (all ≅ = rhombus)
If both rectangle and rhombus: it's a square (the "perfect" quadrilateral)
For trapezoids: check if legs are congruent (isosceles) or not
Memorize the properties table — it's the key to solving problems quickly

examples.title: Classifying a Quadrilateral
examples.text:
A shape has: 4 sides, opposite sides parallel AND equal, all angles 90°.

Step 1: 4 sides → quadrilateral ✓
Step 2: Opposite sides parallel → parallelogram ✓
Step 3: All angles 90° → rectangle ✓

Since it's a parallelogram with right angles but sides are NOT all equal,
it's a rectangle (but not a square).

examples.title: Diagonal Properties of a Square
examples.text:
A square has diagonals that are:

• Congruent (same length) ✓ (rectangle property)
• Perpendicular (meet at 90°) ✓ (rhombus property)
• Bisect each other ✓ (parallelogram property)
• Bisect the angles ✓ (rhombus property)

A square combines ALL diagonal properties!

lessons.tip: Think of the quadrilateral family as a hierarchy: Square ⊂ Rectangle ⊂ Parallelogram ⊂ Quadrilateral. A square is the most special — it has ALL the properties of rectangles, rhombuses, and parallelograms combined. When a problem gives you a square, you can use any of those properties!

quiz.q: Which quadrilateral has ALL sides congruent and ALL angles 90°?
quiz.explanation: A square has all sides congruent (like a rhombus) AND all angles 90° (like a rectangle). It's the most special parallelogram!

quiz.q: A trapezoid has how many pairs of parallel sides?
quiz.explanation: A trapezoid has exactly ONE pair of parallel sides (called bases). Two pairs would make it a parallelogram.

quiz.q: Which quadrilateral has diagonals that are perpendicular and bisect each other?
quiz.explanation: A rhombus has diagonals that are perpendicular AND bisect each other. (A square also has this property since it's a special rhombus.)

lessons.title: Polygons
lessons.description: Classify polygons and find interior and exterior angle measures.
lessons.formula:
Sum of interior angles = (n − 2) × 180°

Each interior angle (regular polygon) = (n − 2) × 180° / n

Sum of exterior angles = 360°

Each exterior angle (regular) = 360° / n

Number of diagonals = n(n − 3) / 2
lessons.content:
A polygon is a closed two-dimensional figure formed by three or more line segments (sides) that meet only at their endpoints (vertices). Polygons are classified by the number of sides: triangle (3), quadrilateral (4), pentagon (5), hexagon (6), heptagon (7), octagon (8), and so on. A polygon with n sides is called an n-gon.

The most important formula in polygon geometry is the interior angle sum: (n − 2) × 180°. This formula works because any polygon can be divided into (n − 2) triangles by drawing diagonals from one vertex. For example, a hexagon (n = 6) has (6 − 2) × 180° = 720° as its interior angle sum. In a regular polygon (all sides and angles equal), each interior angle equals this sum divided by n.

Polygons are convex if all interior angles are less than 180° (no indentations) and concave if at least one interior angle exceeds 180°. The sum of exterior angles of any convex polygon is always 360°, regardless of the number of sides. The number of diagonals in an n-gon is n(n − 3)/2.
steps: Count the number of sides (n) of the polygon.
To find the interior angle sum, apply: (n − 2) × 180°.
For a regular polygon's individual interior angle, divide the sum by n.
To find an exterior angle of a regular polygon: 360° / n.
To count diagonals from one vertex: n − 3. Total diagonals: n(n − 3)/2.
Verify: interior angle + exterior angle = 180° for each vertex.

examples.title: Finding Interior Angles of a Regular Octagon
examples.text:
A regular octagon has 8 sides. Find the measure of each interior angle.

Sum = (8 − 2) × 180° = 6 × 180° = 1080°
Each angle = 1080° / 8 = 135°

examples.title: Counting Diagonals in a Hexagon
examples.text:
How many diagonals does a hexagon have?

Using n(n − 3)/2:
= 6(6 − 3)/2
= 6 × 3 / 2
= 9 diagonals

lessons.tip: The interior angle sum formula (n−2)×180° is one of the most frequently tested geometry formulas. Remember: the '−2' comes from the fact that drawing diagonals from one vertex always creates (n−2) triangles, and each triangle has 180°.

quiz.q: What is the sum of the interior angles of a decagon (10 sides)?
Each interior angle of a regular pentagon measures:
The sum of exterior angles of any convex polygon is always:
quiz.explanation: The sum of the exterior angles of any convex polygon is always 360°, regardless of the number of sides.

lessons.title: Parallelograms
lessons.description: Learn properties of parallelograms.
lessons.formula:
Area = base × height (A = bh)

Perimeter = 2(base + side)

Properties:
• Opposite sides are congruent and parallel
• Opposite angles are congruent
• Consecutive angles are supplementary (sum = 180°)
• Diagonals bisect each other
lessons.content:
A parallelogram is a quadrilateral with both pairs of opposite sides parallel. This single condition creates a rich set of properties: opposite sides are congruent, opposite angles are congruent, consecutive angles are supplementary (add up to 180°), and the diagonals bisect each other (they cross at their midpoints). These properties are frequently used in proofs and problem-solving.

Every rectangle, rhombus, and square is a special type of parallelogram. To prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram, you can show: (1) both pairs of opposite sides are parallel, (2) both pairs of opposite sides are congruent, (3) one pair of sides is both parallel and congruent, (4) both pairs of opposite angles are congruent, (5) consecutive angles are supplementary, or (6) the diagonals bisect each other.

The area of a parallelogram is base × height, where the height is the perpendicular distance between the bases — NOT the length of the slanted side. A common mistake is using the side length instead of the perpendicular height. You can find the height using trigonometry if you know a side length and an interior angle: height = side × sin(angle).
steps: Identify the parallelogram and label its vertices (A, B, C, D in order).
Use properties to find unknown sides or angles (opposite sides/angles are equal).
For area, identify the base and the perpendicular height (not the slant side).
Calculate area = base × height.
For perimeter, add all four sides or use 2(base + side).
If diagonals are involved, use the bisection property: diagonals intersect at their midpoints.

examples.title: Finding Missing Angles
examples.text:
In parallelogram ABCD, angle A = 72°. Find angles B, C, and D.

Opposite angles are congruent:
∠A = ∠C = 72°
Consecutive angles are supplementary:
∠B = 180° − 72° = 108°
∠D = ∠B = 108°

examples.title: Finding Area
examples.text:
A parallelogram has base = 14 cm and height = 9 cm. Find the area.

Area = base × height = 14 × 9 = 126 cm²

lessons.tip: Memorize the 6 ways to prove a quadrilateral is a parallelogram. In coordinate geometry, the quickest method is to check if the midpoints of both diagonals are the same point (proving diagonals bisect each other).

quiz.q: In a parallelogram, if one angle measures 65°, what does the opposite angle measure?
quiz.explanation: Opposite angles in a parallelogram are congruent, so the opposite angle also measures 65°.

quiz.q: The diagonals of a parallelogram always:
quiz.explanation: In any parallelogram, the diagonals always bisect each other (cross at their midpoints).

quiz.q: A parallelogram has base 20 and height 8. What is its area?
quiz.explanation: Area = base × height = 20 × 8 = 160 square units.

lessons.title: Rectangles
lessons.description: Study rectangle properties and theorems.
lessons.formula:
Area = length × width (A = lw)

Perimeter = 2(length + width)

Diagonal = √(l² + w²)  (Pythagorean theorem)

Properties:
• All angles are 90° right angles
• Opposite sides are congruent and parallel
• Diagonals are congruent and bisect each other
lessons.content:
A rectangle is a parallelogram with four right angles. This extra condition gives rectangles additional properties beyond those of a general parallelogram: all four angles are 90°, opposite sides are equal and parallel, and the diagonals are congruent (equal in length) and still bisect each other. Every square is a rectangle, but not every rectangle is a square.

The area of a rectangle is simply length × width. The perimeter is 2(length + width). To find the diagonal length, use the Pythagorean theorem since the diagonal splits the rectangle into two congruent right triangles: diagonal = √(l² + w²). If a rectangle has length 8 and width 6, its diagonal is √(64 + 36) = √100 = 10.

Rectangles are among the most common shapes in real life — doors, screens, books, rooms, and fields are often rectangular. In coordinate geometry, you can prove a quadrilateral is a rectangle by showing it is a parallelogram with congruent diagonals, or by showing it has three right angles (which forces the fourth to also be 90°).
steps: Identify the rectangle and label length (l) and width (w).
Use opposite-sides-congruent property to find missing side lengths.
For area: A = l × w.
For perimeter: P = 2(l + w).
For the diagonal: use d = √(l² + w²) or apply the Pythagorean theorem to one of the right triangles.
To prove a shape is a rectangle: verify all four angles are 90°, or show it is a parallelogram with congruent diagonals.

examples.title: Finding the Diagonal
examples.text:
A rectangle has length 15 m and width 8 m. Find the diagonal.

d = √(15² + 8²) = √(225 + 64) = √289 = 17 m

examples.title: Area and Perimeter
examples.text:
A rectangle has length 24 cm and width 10 cm. Find its area and perimeter.

Area = 24 × 10 = 240 cm²
Perimeter = 2(24 + 10) = 2 × 34 = 68 cm

lessons.tip: The key property that distinguishes a rectangle from a general parallelogram is that its diagonals are congruent. If you know a quadrilateral is a parallelogram AND its diagonals are equal, it must be a rectangle.

quiz.q: A rectangle has length 9 and width 12. What is the length of its diagonal?
Which property is true for rectangles but NOT for all parallelograms?
quiz.explanation: Congruent diagonals are unique to rectangles (and squares). General parallelograms do not necessarily have equal diagonals.

quiz.q: The area of a rectangle with diagonal 10 and width 6 is:

lessons.title: Rhombuses
lessons.description: Study rhombus properties and theorems.
lessons.formula:
Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂
(where d₁ and d₂ are diagonal lengths)

Perimeter = 4 × side

Properties:
• All four sides are congruent
• Opposite angles are congruent
• Diagonals are perpendicular
• Diagonals bisect each other
• Diagonals bisect the angles
lessons.content:
A rhombus is a parallelogram with all four sides congruent (equal in length). Sometimes called a diamond shape, the rhombus has several distinctive properties: all sides are equal, opposite angles are equal, the diagonals are perpendicular (meet at 90°), the diagonals bisect each other, and each diagonal bisects a pair of opposite angles. Every square is a rhombus, but not every rhombus is a square.

The area of a rhombus can be found two ways: (1) using the diagonal formula A = ½ × d₁ × d₂, where d₁ and d₂ are the lengths of the two diagonals, or (2) using base × height like any parallelogram. The diagonal formula is often more convenient because the diagonals are easy to measure or calculate.

The diagonals of a rhombus create four congruent right triangles. Each triangle has legs equal to half of each diagonal and a hypotenuse equal to the side of the rhombus. This relationship (side² = (d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)²) is frequently tested and is derived directly from the Pythagorean theorem applied to one of those right triangles.
steps: Verify the shape is a rhombus (all sides equal, or it is a parallelogram with perpendicular diagonals).
Label the diagonals as d₁ and d₂.
For area using diagonals: A = ½ × d₁ × d₂.
For perimeter: P = 4s (since all four sides are equal).
To find a side length from the diagonals: s = √((d₁/2)² + (d₂/2)²).
Use angle-bisection properties to find angle measures: each diagonal splits its vertex angles in half.

examples.title: Area Using Diagonals
examples.text:
A rhombus has diagonals of length 16 cm and 10 cm. Find the area.

A = ½ × d₁ × d₂ = ½ × 16 × 10 = 80 cm²

examples.title: Finding the Side Length
examples.text:
A rhombus has diagonals of 14 m and 12 m. Find the side length.

Each half-diagonal: 7 and 6
s = √(7² + 6²) = √(49 + 36) = √85 ≈ 9.22 m

lessons.tip: The area formula A = ½d₁d₂ is the fastest way to find a rhombus's area. Also remember: a rhombus is a parallelogram with ALL sides equal. If you need to prove something is a rhombus, show all sides are congruent or show the diagonals are perpendicular bisectors of each other.

quiz.q: A rhombus has diagonals of 18 and 24. What is its area?
quiz.explanation: A = ½ × 18 × 24 = ½ × 432 = 216 square units.

quiz.q: The diagonals of a rhombus always:
options: Have the same length as the sides
quiz.explanation: The diagonals of a rhombus are always perpendicular to each other.

quiz.q: If a rhombus has diagonals of 10 and 24, what is its perimeter?
quiz.explanation: Half-diagonals: 5 and 12. Side = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13. Perimeter = 4 × 13 = 52.

lessons.title: Squares
lessons.description: Understand squares as special rectangles and rhombuses.
lessons.formula:
Area = s²

Perimeter = 4s

Diagonal = s√2

Properties (combines rectangle + rhombus):
• All sides congruent
• All angles are 90°
• Diagonals are congruent, perpendicular, and bisect angles
• Diagonals bisect each other
lessons.content:
A square is the most special quadrilateral — it combines all the properties of a rectangle AND a rhombus. A square is a parallelogram with four congruent sides and four right angles. Its diagonals are congruent (like a rectangle), perpendicular (like a rhombus), and they bisect the angles (like a rhombus). A square is sometimes called a regular quadrilateral because all sides and all angles are equal.

The formulas for a square are the simplest of all quadrilaterals. Area = s² (side squared), Perimeter = 4s, and Diagonal = s√2. The diagonal formula comes from the Pythagorean theorem applied to the right triangle formed by two adjacent sides and the diagonal: d = √(s² + s²) = s√2.

In proofs, to show a quadrilateral is a square, you must prove it is BOTH a rectangle and a rhombus. For example, show that all four sides are equal (rhombus property) and the diagonals are congruent (rectangle property), or show that it is a parallelogram with one right angle and all sides equal.
steps: Verify the shape is a square: all sides equal AND all angles 90°.
For area: A = s², or A = ½ × d² (using diagonal).
For perimeter: P = 4s.
For diagonal: d = s√2, or s = d/√2.
Use diagonal properties in proofs: diagonals are congruent, perpendicular, and bisect angles.
When solving problems, leverage both rectangle and rhombus properties freely.

examples.title: Finding the Diagonal
examples.text:
A square has side length 12 cm. Find its diagonal.

d = s√2 = 12√2 ≈ 16.97 cm

examples.title: Finding Side from Diagonal
examples.text:
A square has a diagonal of 20 inches. Find its area.

s = d/√2 = 20/√2 = 10√2 ≈ 14.14 in
Area = s² = (10√2)² = 200 in²

lessons.tip: A square inherits ALL properties from rectangles, rhombuses, and parallelograms. In proofs, the most efficient way to prove a shape is a square is to prove it is a rhombus with one right angle, or a rectangle with all sides equal.

quiz.q: The diagonal of a square with side 10 is:
Which properties does a square have that a rhombus does NOT?
options: All sides congruent and diagonals perpendicular
Diagonals bisect each other and bisect angles
Opposite sides parallel and opposite angles congruent
quiz.explanation: A rhombus does not necessarily have 90° angles or congruent diagonals. A square has both.

quiz.q: The area of a square with diagonal 8√2 is:

lessons.title: Trapezoids
lessons.description: Learn properties of trapezoids and isosceles trapezoids.
lessons.formula:
Area = ½(b₁ + b₂) × h

Median length = ½(b₁ + b₂)

Properties:
• Exactly one pair of parallel sides (bases)
• Isosceles: legs congruent, base angles congruent
• Median is parallel to bases and equals their average
lessons.content:
A trapezoid is a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides. The parallel sides are called the bases (b₁ and b₂), and the non-parallel sides are called the legs. The perpendicular distance between the bases is the height (h). The area formula for a trapezoid is A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h, which essentially averages the two bases and multiplies by the height.

An isosceles trapezoid has congruent legs, which creates additional properties: the base angles of each base are congruent, and the diagonals are congruent. A right trapezoid has one leg perpendicular to the bases, making that leg equal to the height. The median (or midsegment) of a trapezoid connects the midpoints of the legs; it is parallel to the bases and its length equals the average of the bases: m = ½(b₁ + b₂).

In coordinate geometry problems, trapezoids often appear with horizontal bases. To find the height, use the vertical distance between the parallel lines. For non-horizontal trapezoids, you may need to drop a perpendicular from one vertex to the opposite base to create a right triangle and find the height using the Pythagorean theorem.
steps: Identify the two parallel sides (bases b₁ and b₂) and the height h.
If the height is not given, find it by dropping a perpendicular from one base to the other.
Calculate the area: A = ½(b₁ + b₂) × h.
For the median: find midpoints of both legs and connect them, or use m = ½(b₁ + b₂).
For isosceles trapezoids, use congruent legs and base angles to find unknown values.
For perimeter: add all four sides together (b₁ + b₂ + leg₁ + leg₂).

examples.title: Finding the Area of a Trapezoid
examples.text:
A trapezoid has bases of 12 cm and 20 cm, and height of 7 cm. Find the area.

A = ½(b₁ + b₂) × h = ½(12 + 20) × 7 = ½ × 32 × 7 = 112 cm²

examples.title: Finding the Median
examples.text:
An isosceles trapezoid has bases 15 in and 25 in. Find the length of the median.

Median = ½(b₁ + b₂) = ½(15 + 25) = ½ × 40 = 20 in

lessons.tip: Think of the trapezoid area formula as 'average the bases, then multiply by height.' The median formula is the same average of the bases. Many trapezoid problems on tests require you to find the height first by creating right triangles with perpendiculars dropped from the shorter base.

quiz.q: A trapezoid has bases 8 and 14 with height 5. What is its area?
The median of a trapezoid with bases 10 and 22 is:
Which is true for an isosceles trapezoid but NOT for all trapezoids?
quiz.explanation: Congruent legs are specific to isosceles trapezoids. General trapezoids can have unequal legs.

lessons.title: Kites
lessons.description: Study kite properties and theorems.
lessons.formula:
Area = ½ × d₁ × d₂
(where d₁ and d₂ are diagonal lengths)

Perimeter = 2(a + b)
(where a and b are the lengths of two pairs of congruent sides)

Properties:
• Two pairs of adjacent congruent sides
• One diagonal bisects the other
• Diagonals are perpendicular
• One diagonal bisects vertex angles
lessons.content:
A kite is a quadrilateral with two pairs of adjacent sides that are congruent. Think of the shape of a traditional flying kite: it has a vertical axis of symmetry. The longer diagonal (the axis of symmetry) bisects the shorter diagonal at a right angle and also bisects the vertex angles at its endpoints.

The area of a kite is found using the same diagonal formula as a rhombus: A = ½ × d₁ × d₂. The perpendicular diagonals create four right triangles within the kite, and each pair of opposite triangles is congruent. If you know the side lengths and one diagonal, you can find the other diagonal using the Pythagorean theorem.

Kites share properties with rhombuses (perpendicular diagonals, diagonal bisection), but unlike rhombuses, a kite does NOT have all sides equal and its diagonals are NOT congruent. A rhombus is actually a special kite where all four sides are equal. When solving kite problems, focus on the right triangles formed by the diagonals and apply the Pythagorean theorem.
steps: Identify the kite and label its two pairs of congruent adjacent sides.
Label the diagonals: the symmetry axis (longer) and the cross diagonal (shorter).
For area: A = ½ × d₁ × d₂.
Use the Pythagorean theorem with half-diagonals to find side lengths or missing diagonal segments.
Use the bisection properties: the long diagonal bisects the short diagonal and the vertex angles.
For perimeter: P = 2(a + b), where a and b are the two different side lengths.

examples.title: Finding Area of a Kite
examples.text:
A kite has diagonals of length 18 cm and 10 cm. Find its area.

A = ½ × d₁ × d₂ = ½ × 18 × 10 = 90 cm²

examples.title: Finding Side Lengths
examples.text:
A kite has diagonals of 16 and 12. Find the side lengths.

Half-diagonals: 8 and 6
Each side pair forms right triangles with legs 6 and 8.
Side = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10
(If different triangles, each side = √(half-d₁² + half-d₂²))

lessons.tip: Kites and rhombuses share the area formula A = ½d₁d₂. The key difference: a kite has TWO pairs of adjacent equal sides, while a rhombus has ALL four sides equal. In problems, the perpendicular diagonals always create right triangles — use the Pythagorean theorem liberally.

quiz.q: A kite has diagonals of 14 and 20. What is its area?
quiz.explanation: A = ½ × 14 × 20 = 140 square units.

quiz.q: In a kite, the longer diagonal always:
options: Is equal to the shorter diagonal
Bisects the shorter diagonal at a right angle
Is perpendicular to the shorter diagonal but does not bisect it
quiz.explanation: The longer diagonal (axis of symmetry) bisects the shorter diagonal and does so at a right angle.

quiz.q: A kite has diagonals 10 and 24. What is the perimeter if all four right triangles are congruent?
quiz.explanation: Half-diagonals: 5 and 12. Side = √(25+144) = √169 = 13. If all 4 triangles are congruent (rhombus), P = 4 × 13 = 52.

lessons.title: Circle Basics
lessons.description: Learn radius, diameter, and circumference.
lessons.formula:
Diameter: d = 2r

Circumference: C = 2πr = πd

Area: A = πr²

Radius from diameter: r = d/2

Key relationships:
• d = 2r
• Longest chord = diameter
• Tangent ⊥ radius at point of tangency
lessons.content:
A circle is the set of all points in a plane that are equidistant from a fixed point called the center. The distance from the center to any point on the circle is the radius (r). The diameter (d) passes through the center and equals 2r. The circumference is the distance around the circle, calculated as C = 2πr or C = πd. The area is A = πr².

A chord is a line segment whose endpoints lie on the circle. The diameter is the longest possible chord. A secant is a line that intersects the circle at two points (it contains a chord). A tangent is a line that touches the circle at exactly one point, called the point of tangency. A critical theorem states that a tangent line is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency.

In the coordinate plane, a circle with center (h, k) and radius r has the equation (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r². This standard form is essential for analytical geometry problems. The unit circle (radius = 1, centered at origin) is the foundation of trigonometry.
