steps: Identify the center and radius (or diameter) of the circle.
If given the diameter, find the radius: r = d/2.
For circumference: C = 2πr (or πd if diameter is given).
For area: A = πr².
For a tangent line problem, draw the radius to the point of tangency — it creates a right angle with the tangent.
Use the Pythagorean theorem when combining radii, chords, and tangent segments.

examples.title: Finding Circumference and Area
examples.text:
A circle has a radius of 7 cm. Find its circumference and area.

C = 2πr = 2π(7) = 14π ≈ 43.98 cm
A = πr² = π(49) = 49π ≈ 153.94 cm²

examples.title: Using the Tangent-Radius Theorem
examples.text:
Line AB is tangent to circle O at point A. If the radius OA = 5 and point B is 13 units from the center O, find AB.

Since tangent ⊥ radius: ∠OAB = 90°
Using Pythagorean theorem:
AB² + 5² = 13²
AB² = 169 − 25 = 144
AB = 12

lessons.tip: The tangent-radius perpendicularity is one of the most tested circle theorems. Whenever you see a tangent line, immediately draw the radius to the point of tangency to create a right angle. This gives you a right triangle to work with.

quiz.q: A circle has a diameter of 16 cm. What is its circumference?
quiz.explanation: C = πd = π(16) = 16π cm.

quiz.q: A tangent line to a circle is always perpendicular to what?
options: The radius at the point of tangency
quiz.explanation: A tangent line is perpendicular to the radius drawn to the point of tangency.

quiz.q: The area of a circle with radius 10 is:

lessons.title: Arcs
lessons.description: Measure and classify arcs in circles.
lessons.formula:
Arc length = (θ / 360°) × 2πr
or
Arc length = (θ / 360°) × πd

where θ = central angle in degrees

Minor arc: measure < 180°
Major arc: measure > 180°
Semicircle: measure = 180°

Major arc measure = 360° − minor arc measure
lessons.content:
An arc is a portion of the circumference of a circle. Arcs are classified by their measure (the degree measure of their central angle). A minor arc has a measure less than 180°, a semicircle equals exactly 180°, and a major arc exceeds 180°. Arcs are named with two or three points: a minor arc uses two endpoints (arc AB), while a major arc uses three points to avoid ambiguity (arc ACB).

The arc measure equals the measure of its central angle — it is an angle measurement in degrees, not a length. The arc length is the actual physical distance along the circle, calculated as a fraction of the total circumference: arc length = (θ/360°) × 2πr. For example, a 90° arc in a circle of radius 6 has length (90/360) × 12π = 3π ≈ 9.42.

Congruent arcs have the same measure AND are in the same circle (or congruent circles). Two minor arcs in the same circle are congruent if and only if their corresponding chords are congruent. This bidirectional relationship between chords and arcs is fundamental to many circle proofs.
steps: Identify the arc's endpoints and the central angle that intercepts it.
Determine if the arc is minor (< 180°) or major (> 180°).
For arc measure: it equals the central angle θ in degrees.
For arc length: apply L = (θ/360°) × 2πr.
For a major arc, use the three-point naming convention (e.g., arc ACB).
To find an arc's measure when given the minor arc, subtract from 360°.

examples.title: Finding Arc Length
examples.text:
A circle has radius 12 cm. Find the length of a 75° arc.

L = (75/360) × 2π(12)
L = (5/24) × 24π = 5π ≈ 15.71 cm

examples.title: Finding Major Arc Measure
examples.text:
Minor arc AB = 110°. Find major arc ACB.

Major arc ACB = 360° − 110° = 250°

lessons.tip: Don't confuse arc measure (in degrees) with arc length (a distance). Arc measure equals the central angle; arc length is a fraction of the circumference. Also remember: two chords are congruent if and only if their minor arcs are congruent (same circle).

quiz.q: Find the length of a 60° arc in a circle of radius 9.
If minor arc AB = 130°, what is major arc ACB?
The measure of an arc equals the measure of its:
quiz.explanation: The measure of an arc equals the measure of the central angle that intercepts it.

lessons.title: Central Angles
lessons.description: Understand central angles and their relationship to arcs.
lessons.formula:
Central angle = intercepted arc measure

θ = arc measure (in degrees)

Arc length = (θ / 360°) × 2πr

Properties:
• Vertex is at the center of the circle
• Measure equals the intercepted arc
• Congruent central angles intercept congruent arcs
• Sum of central angles around center = 360°
lessons.content:
A central angle is an angle whose vertex is at the center of a circle and whose sides (rays) intersect the circle. The fundamental theorem of central angles states that the measure of a central angle equals the measure of its intercepted arc. If central angle AOB measures 70°, then arc AB also measures 70°. This one-to-one correspondence is the foundation of arc-angle relationships in circle geometry.

Central angles have important properties: congruent central angles intercept congruent arcs (and vice versa), the sum of all central angles around a point is 360°, and a central angle that intercepts a semicircle measures 180°. When multiple central angles share the circle, you can set up equations using the 360° total to find unknown angles or arc measures.

In applications, central angles appear in pie charts, clock problems, gear ratios, and navigation. A clock's minute hand, for example, creates a 6° central angle each minute (360°/60 = 6° per minute). Central angles are also essential for understanding inscribed angles, which always measure exactly half of their intercepted central angle.
steps: Identify the central angle: its vertex must be at the center of the circle.
Determine the intercepted arc (the arc between the two points where the angle's sides meet the circle).
Set the central angle equal to the intercepted arc measure: θ = arc measure.
If other central angles are present, use the fact that they sum to 360°.
For arc length problems, use L = (θ/360°) × 2πr.
In proofs, use the congruence principle: equal central angles ↔ equal arcs.

examples.title: Finding Arc Measure from Central Angle
examples.text:
Central angle AOB measures 120° in circle O. What is the measure of arc AB?

Arc AB = ∠AOB = 120°

examples.title: Using Central Angles to Find Unknown Arcs
examples.text:
Three central angles in a circle measure 85°, 110°, and x°. Find x.

All central angles sum to 360°:
85 + 110 + x = 360
195 + x = 360
x = 165°

lessons.tip: The key rule: central angle = intercepted arc. This is the most fundamental relationship in circle geometry and the basis for the inscribed angle theorem. If you see a central angle, immediately write 'angle = arc' as your starting point.

quiz.q: A central angle measures 135°. What is its intercepted arc?
quiz.explanation: The intercepted arc of a central angle has the same measure as the angle: 135°.

quiz.q: Two central angles in the same circle are congruent. Their intercepted arcs are:
quiz.explanation: Congruent central angles intercept congruent arcs in the same circle (or congruent circles).

quiz.q: The minute hand of a clock moves from the 12 to the 3. What central angle does it sweep?
quiz.explanation: From 12 to 3 is 3 hour marks out of 12, so 3/12 × 360° = 90°.

lessons.title: Inscribed Angles
lessons.description: Learn the Inscribed Angle Theorem.
lessons.formula:
Inscribed angle = ½ × intercepted arc

∠inscribed = ½ × arc measure

Corollaries:
• Angle inscribed in a semicircle = 90°
• Inscribed angles intercepting the same arc are congruent
• Opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral are supplementary (sum = 180°)
lessons.content:
An inscribed angle is an angle whose vertex lies on the circle and whose sides contain chords of the circle. The Inscribed Angle Theorem is one of the most important theorems in circle geometry: the measure of an inscribed angle is exactly half the measure of its intercepted arc. If inscribed angle ABC intercepts arc AC measuring 100°, then angle ABC = 50°.

Three important corollaries follow from this theorem. First, an angle inscribed in a semicircle (intercepting a 180° arc) always measures 90° — this is Thales' Theorem. Second, any two inscribed angles that intercept the same arc are congruent (they each equal half the arc). Third, the opposite angles of a cyclic quadrilateral (one inscribed in a circle) are supplementary, summing to 180°.

In problem-solving, when you see an angle with its vertex on the circle, immediately check what arc it intercepts. If the arc measure is known, halve it for the inscribed angle. If the inscribed angle is known, double it for the intercepted arc. This theorem connects angles and arcs and is the key to solving most circle angle problems.
steps: Identify the inscribed angle: vertex must be ON the circle (not at the center).
Determine the intercepted arc: the arc between the two chord endpoints that lies in the interior of the angle.
Apply the Inscribed Angle Theorem: inscribed angle = ½ × intercepted arc.
If the angle intercepts a semicircle (diameter as one side), the angle is 90°.
For two inscribed angles intercepting the same arc, set them equal to each other.
In a cyclic quadrilateral, use opposite angles supplementary: ∠A + ∠C = 180° and ∠B + ∠D = 180°.

examples.title: Finding an Inscribed Angle
examples.text:
In circle O, inscribed angle ABC intercepts arc AC = 140°. Find angle ABC.

∠ABC = ½ × arc AC = ½ × 140° = 70°

examples.title: Using Thales' Theorem
examples.text:
Points A, B, C are on a circle where AC is a diameter. What is angle ABC?

Since AC is a diameter, arc AC = 180°.
∠ABC is inscribed in a semicircle, so ∠ABC = ½ × 180° = 90°

lessons.tip: The Inscribed Angle Theorem (angle = half arc) is the #1 tool for circle angle problems. Whenever you see an angle on the circle, ask: 'What arc does it intercept?' If a problem involves a diameter, the inscribed angle opposite it is always 90° — no calculation needed.

quiz.q: An inscribed angle intercepts an arc of 110°. What is the angle's measure?
quiz.explanation: Inscribed angle = ½ × intercepted arc = ½ × 110° = 55°.

quiz.q: An angle inscribed in a semicircle always measures:
quiz.explanation: A semicircle arc = 180°, so the inscribed angle = ½ × 180° = 90°. This is Thales' Theorem.

quiz.q: Two inscribed angles intercept the same arc of 80°. What is each angle?
quiz.explanation: Both angles = ½ × 80° = 40°. Inscribed angles intercepting the same arc are congruent.

lessons.title: Chords and Tangents
lessons.description: Study chord and tangent properties.
lessons.formula:
Chord-Chord Power Theorem:
a × b = c × d
(products of segment lengths are equal)

Tangent-Tangent segments from external point:
Both tangent segments are congruent

Chord distance from center:
d² + (c/2)² = r²
where d = distance from center to chord, c = chord length
lessons.content:
Chord properties and tangent properties are fundamental to circle geometry. Key chord theorems include: (1) The perpendicular from the center to a chord bisects the chord — if a radius is perpendicular to a chord, it cuts the chord in half; conversely, a line from the center to the midpoint of a chord is perpendicular to it. (2) Congruent chords are equidistant from the center — chords of the same length are the same distance from the center. (3) If two chords are different distances from the center, the closer chord is longer.

When two chords intersect inside a circle, the Intersecting Chords Theorem (Power of a Point) states that the products of their segment lengths are equal: if chord AB and chord CD intersect at point P, then AP × PB = CP × PD. This powerful theorem lets you find unknown segment lengths when chords cross.

For tangents, the key theorems are: (1) A tangent is perpendicular to the radius at the point of tangency. (2) Two tangent segments drawn from the same external point to a circle are congruent. This means if two tangents touch a circle from point P, both tangent segments from P to their respective points of tangency have the same length. These properties combine frequently in problems involving right triangles and the Pythagorean theorem.
steps: For chord problems: draw the perpendicular from the center to the chord, creating a right triangle.
Use the Pythagorean theorem with radius, half-chord, and distance from center: r² = d² + (c/2)².
For intersecting chords: apply AP × PB = CP × PD.
For tangent problems: draw the radius to the point of tangency (creates a right angle).
If two tangents come from the same external point, set their lengths equal.
Combine multiple theorems for complex problems: tangent ⊥ radius + Pythagorean theorem + chord properties.

examples.title: Finding Chord Length from Distance to Center
examples.text:
A chord is 6 units from the center of a circle with radius 10. Find the chord length.

Using right triangle: r² = d² + (c/2)²
10² = 6² + (c/2)²
100 = 36 + (c/2)²
(c/2)² = 64, so c/2 = 8
c = 16

examples.title: Intersecting Chords Theorem
examples.text:
Two chords intersect inside a circle. One chord is divided into segments of 4 and 6. The other chord has one segment of 3. Find the other segment.

AP × PB = CP × PD
4 × 6 = 3 × x
24 = 3x
x = 8

lessons.tip: The intersecting chords theorem (AP × PB = CP × PD) is one of the most powerful tools in circle geometry. Memorize it as 'the products of the two segments of each chord are equal.' For tangent problems, always draw the radius to create a right triangle.

quiz.q: A chord is 8 units from the center of a circle with radius 17. What is half the chord length?
Two chords intersect. Segments are 5×8 and 4×x. What is x?
Two tangent segments from the same external point to a circle are always:
quiz.explanation: Two tangent segments drawn from the same external point to a circle are always congruent in length.

lessons.title: Secants
lessons.description: Understand secant lines and secant-tangent relationships.
lessons.formula:
Secant-Secant Power Theorem:
external₁ × whole₁ = external₂ × whole₂
(a)(a + b) = (c)(c + d)

Secant-Tangent Power Theorem:
(tangent segment)² = (external)(whole secant)
t² = a(a + b)

where 'external' is the part outside the circle
and 'whole' is the entire secant length
lessons.content:
A secant is a line that intersects a circle at exactly two points. Unlike a chord (which is a segment inside the circle), a secant extends beyond the circle on both sides. The portion of a secant outside the circle is called the external segment, and the portion inside is the internal segment. The Power of a Point theorems for secants relate the lengths of these segments.

The Secant-Secant Theorem states that when two secants intersect outside a circle, the product of the external segment and the entire secant length is the same for both secants: external₁ × whole₁ = external₂ × whole₂. For example, if one secant has external part 3 and whole length 12 (so internal = 9), and another has external part 4 and internal part x, then 3 × 12 = 4 × (4 + x), giving 36 = 16 + 4x, so x = 5.

The Secant-Tangent Theorem applies when a secant and a tangent meet at an external point. It states that the square of the tangent segment equals the product of the external secant segment and the whole secant: tangent² = external × whole. This is a special case of the more general Power of a Point concept. The angle formed by two secants, two tangents, or a secant and a tangent is always half the difference of their intercepted arcs.
steps: Identify the external point where secants (or a secant and tangent) meet.
Label the external segment and the whole secant length for each line.
For secant-secant: apply external₁ × whole₁ = external₂ × whole₂.
For secant-tangent: apply tangent² = external × whole secant.
Set up the equation and solve for the unknown segment length.
For angle problems: the angle formed = ½(larger intercepted arc − smaller intercepted arc).

examples.title: Secant-Secant Theorem
examples.text:
Two secants intersect outside a circle. Secant PA has external part PA = 4 and reaches the circle at A then B (so PB = 16 total). Secant PC has external part PC = 6. Find PD (whole secant).

PA × PB = PC × PD
4 × 16 = 6 × PD
64 = 6 × PD
PD = 64/6 ≈ 10.67

examples.title: Secant-Tangent Theorem
examples.text:
A tangent segment PT = 8 and a secant from the same point P has external part PA = 4. Find the whole secant PB.

PT² = PA × PB
8² = 4 × PB
64 = 4 × PB
PB = 16

lessons.tip: All three Power of a Point formulas follow the same pattern: the product of the full segment and its external part is constant. For intersecting chords (inside), it's segment × segment. For secant-secant (outside), it's external × whole. For secant-tangent (outside), it's tangent² = external × whole. Think of tangent as a secant where external = whole.

quiz.q: Two secants from point P: PA = 5, PB = 20, PC = 4. Find PD (whole secant from P through D).
A tangent of length 6 and a secant with external part 3 meet at the same point. What is the whole secant length?
quiz.explanation: 6² = 3 × whole → 36 = 3 × whole → whole = 12.

quiz.q: The angle formed by two secants intersecting outside a circle equals:
options: Half the sum of intercepted arcs
Half the difference of intercepted arcs
quiz.explanation: The angle formed by two secants, two tangents, or a secant and tangent outside a circle equals ½(larger arc − smaller arc).

lessons.title: Arc Length and Sector Area
lessons.description: Calculate arc length and sector area using proportions of circumference and area!
lessons.formula:
Arc Length = (theta/360) x 2*pi*r
Sector Area = (theta/360) x pi*r^2

Where theta is the central angle in degrees
The fraction of the circle = theta/360
lessons.content:
An arc is a portion of the circumference of a circle, and a sector is a 'pie slice' region bounded by two radii and an arc. Both are found using proportions: the central angle determines what fraction of the full circle you are working with.

For arc length: if the central angle is 90 degrees (a quarter of 360), the arc is a quarter of the full circumference. Arc Length = (90/360) x 2(pi)r = (1/4) x 2(pi)r = (pi)r/2. For a full circle with r=10: circumference = 20(pi), and the 90-degree arc = 5(pi).

Sector area works the same way. A 60-degree sector is 60/360 = 1/6 of the full circle area. Sector Area = (60/360) x (pi)r^2. With r=6: full area = 36(pi), sector = 6(pi). Always convert the angle to a fraction of 360 first, then multiply by the full circumference or area.
steps: Find the central angle (theta) in degrees
Calculate the fraction: theta / 360
For arc length: multiply the fraction by 2*pi*r
For sector area: multiply the fraction by pi*r^2
Include units: arc length in linear units, area in square units

examples.title: Arc Length
examples.text: Central angle 120 degrees, r = 5. Arc = (120/360) x 2(pi)(5) = (1/3) x 10(pi) = 10(pi)/3.

examples.title: Sector Area
examples.text: Central angle 45 degrees, r = 8. Area = (45/360) x (pi)(64) = (1/8) x 64(pi) = 8(pi) square units.

lessons.tip: Think of arc length and sector area as 'portions of the whole.' A 90-degree sector is exactly one-fourth of the circle, just like a quarter of a pizza!

quiz.q: Central angle 180 degrees, r = 6. Arc length?
Central angle 60 degrees, r = 4. Sector area?
A 90-degree arc in a circle of radius 10 is:
quiz.explanation: 90/360 = 1/4. One-fourth of the circumference.

quiz.q: What fraction of a circle is a 270-degree sector?
quiz.explanation: 270/360 = 3/4. Three-fourths of the circle.

lessons.title: Slope
lessons.description: Calculate and interpret slope of lines.
vocabulary: Slope — the steepness of a line, calculated as rise over run between two points
Rise — the vertical change between two points on a line
Run — the horizontal change between two points on a line
Positive slope — a line that goes uphill from left to right
Negative slope — a line that goes downhill from left to right
Zero slope — a horizontal line with no vertical change
Undefined slope — a vertical line with no horizontal change
lessons.formula:
m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁) = rise / run

Positive slope: line rises left to right (m > 0)
Negative slope: line falls left to right (m < 0)
Zero slope: horizontal line (m = 0)
Undefined slope: vertical line (Δx = 0)
lessons.content:
Slope measures the steepness and direction of a line. Given any two points on a line, you can calculate the slope by finding the ratio of the vertical change (rise) to the horizontal change (run). The slope formula m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) is one of the most fundamental formulas in coordinate geometry.

The sign of the slope tells you the direction of the line. A positive slope means the line rises from left to right, a negative slope means it falls, a zero slope indicates a horizontal line, and an undefined slope occurs with vertical lines because division by zero is impossible. Understanding these four cases helps you quickly identify the behavior of any line.

When calculating slope, always be consistent with the order of your points: the same point must be used as the first term in both the numerator and denominator. Swapping points gives the same result, but mixing them up changes the sign of the slope. Practice plotting points and counting rise and run on graph paper to build intuition.
steps: Identify two points on the line and label them (x₁, y₁) and (x₂, y₂)
Find the change in y (rise) by subtracting: y₂ − y₁
Find the change in x (run) by subtracting: x₂ − x₁
Divide the rise by the run to get the slope m
Reduce the fraction to simplest form if possible
Determine the slope type: positive, negative, zero, or undefined

examples.title: Finding Slope from Two Points
examples.text: Find the slope of the line passing through (2, 3) and (6, 11). Using m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (11 − 3)/(6 − 2) = 8/4 = 2. The slope is 2, which is positive, so the line rises from left to right. For every 1 unit of horizontal movement, the line goes up 2 units.

examples.title: Identifying Slope Type
examples.text: Determine the slope of a horizontal line passing through (3, 5) and (8, 5). Since y₂ − y₁ = 5 − 5 = 0, the slope is 0/5 = 0. A zero slope means the line is perfectly horizontal. For a vertical line like x = 4 through points (4, 1) and (4, 7), the run would be 4 − 4 = 0, making the slope undefined.

lessons.tip: Remember the phrase 'rise over run' — the vertical change always goes on top in the numerator. Also, the slope is the same no matter which two points you pick on the line, because a straight line has constant steepness.

quiz.q: What is the slope of the line through (1, 4) and (3, 10)?
A line passes through (5, 7) and (5, −3). What is its slope?
quiz.explanation: The x-values are both 5, so run = 0. Division by zero makes the slope undefined, meaning the line is vertical.

quiz.q: Which type of slope does a line that falls from left to right have?
quiz.explanation: A line falling from left to right has a negative slope because the y-values decrease as x-values increase.

lessons.title: Equations of Lines
lessons.description: Write equations in slope-intercept and point-slope form.
vocabulary: Slope-intercept form — y = mx + b, where m is slope and b is y-intercept
Point-slope form — y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), useful when you know a point and slope
Standard form — Ax + By = C, where A, B, and C are integers and A ≥ 0
Y-intercept — the point where a line crosses the y-axis, where x = 0
X-intercept — the point where a line crosses the x-axis, where y = 0
Linear equation — an equation whose graph is a straight line
Slope — the constant rate of change between any two points on a line
lessons.formula:
Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b
Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Standard form: Ax + By = C

X-intercept: set y = 0, solve for x
Y-intercept: set x = 0, solve for y
lessons.content:
There are three common ways to write the equation of a line, and each form highlights different information. Slope-intercept form (y = mx + b) immediately reveals the slope m and y-intercept b, making it the best choice for graphing. Point-slope form (y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)) is the most efficient way to write an equation when you know the slope and any point on the line. Standard form (Ax + By = C) is useful for certain algebraic operations and is required in many textbook answers.

Converting between forms is a key skill. To go from point-slope to slope-intercept, simply distribute and solve for y. To convert to standard form, rearrange so that x and y terms are on one side and the constant is on the other, then ensure A is non-negative and all coefficients are integers with no common factors.

When a problem gives you two points, first calculate the slope, then substitute the slope and one of the points into point-slope form. From there, you can convert to whichever form the problem requests. Always double-check your equation by plugging both original points back in — if both satisfy the equation, your work is correct.
steps: Determine what information is given: slope, a point, or two points
If two points are given, calculate the slope first using m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)
Substitute the slope and a known point into point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Simplify and solve for y to get slope-intercept form, or rearrange for standard form
Verify by plugging both given points into your equation
State the final answer in the form requested by the problem

examples.title: Writing an Equation from Two Points
examples.text: Write the slope-intercept form of the line through (−1, 3) and (2, −3). First, find the slope: m = (−3 − 3)/(2 − (−1)) = −6/3 = −2. Using point-slope with (2, −3): y − (−3) = −2(x − 2). Simplify: y + 3 = −2x + 4, so y = −2x + 1. Check with (−1, 3): 3 = −2(−1) + 1 = 3. Correct!

examples.title: Converting to Standard Form
examples.text: Convert y = (3/4)x − 5 to standard form. Start by moving the x term: y − (3/4)x = −5. Multiply both sides by 4 to clear the fraction: 4y − 3x = −20. Rearrange so x comes first: −3x + 4y = −20. Since A must be non-negative, multiply by −1: 3x − 4y = 20. This is standard form with A=3, B=−4, C=20.

lessons.tip: Use slope-intercept form (y = mx + b) when graphing because the slope and y-intercept are immediately visible. Use point-slope form as your 'working form' when you need to derive an equation, then convert to whatever the problem requires.

quiz.q: What is the slope-intercept form of the line with slope 4 and y-intercept −7?
quiz.explanation: In y = mx + b, substitute m = 4 and b = −7 to get y = 4x − 7.

quiz.q: Given point (3, 5) and slope −2, which is the correct point-slope form?
quiz.explanation: Point-slope form is y − y₁ = m(x − x₁), so y − 5 = −2(x − 3).

quiz.q: Which equation is in standard form Ax + By = C?
quiz.explanation: Standard form has Ax + By = C with all variable terms on one side. Only 5x − 2y = 8 matches this pattern.

lessons.title: Parallel and Perpendicular Slopes
lessons.description: Use slopes to determine parallel and perpendicular lines.
vocabulary: Parallel lines — lines in the same plane that never intersect; they have equal slopes
Perpendicular lines — lines that intersect at a right angle (90°); slopes are negative reciprocals
Negative reciprocal — two numbers whose product is −1, e.g., 3 and −1/3
Same slope — parallel lines share the exact same slope value
Right angle — a 90° angle formed by perpendicular lines
Transversal — a line that crosses two or more lines
lessons.formula:
Parallel lines: m₁ = m₂ (same slope)
Perpendicular lines: m₁ × m₂ = −1

If m₁ = a/b, then m₂ = −b/a (negative reciprocal)

Horizontal line (m = 0) ⟂ Vertical line (m = undefined)
lessons.content:
The relationship between the slopes of two lines tells you whether they are parallel or perpendicular. Parallel lines have the exact same slope but different y-intercepts — they run alongside each other and never meet. Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals of each other, meaning their product equals −1. If one line has slope 2/3, a perpendicular line has slope −3/2.

To find the equation of a line parallel or perpendicular to a given line, first identify the slope of the original line by rewriting it in slope-intercept form if necessary. For a parallel line, keep the same slope and use the new point to find a different y-intercept. For a perpendicular line, take the negative reciprocal of the slope, then use the given point to find the new y-intercept.

A special case occurs with horizontal and vertical lines. A horizontal line (slope 0) is always perpendicular to a vertical line (undefined slope), even though you cannot calculate a negative reciprocal of zero. Similarly, two horizontal lines are parallel, and two vertical lines are parallel. Always check that parallel lines are truly distinct by verifying they have different y-intercepts.
steps: Rewrite the given line equation in slope-intercept form to find its slope
For parallel lines: keep the same slope m₁ = m₂
For perpendicular lines: flip the slope and change its sign to get the negative reciprocal
Use the given point with the new slope in point-slope form
Simplify to the requested form (slope-intercept or standard)
Verify: parallel lines should have same slope but different intercepts; perpendicular slopes should multiply to −1

examples.title: Parallel Line Through a Point
examples.text: Write the equation of a line parallel to y = −2x + 5 that passes through (4, 1). The slope of the given line is −2, so the parallel line also has slope −2. Using point-slope: y − 1 = −2(x − 4). Simplify: y − 1 = −2x + 8, so y = −2x + 9. Check: slopes are both −2, and y-intercepts (5 and 9) are different. Correct!

examples.title: Perpendicular Line Through a Point
examples.text: Write the equation of a line perpendicular to 3x + 6y = 12 passing through (−2, 5). First, find the slope: 6y = −3x + 12, so y = −(1/2)x + 2. The slope is −1/2, so the perpendicular slope is the negative reciprocal: 2. Using point-slope: y − 5 = 2(x − (−2)), which simplifies to y − 5 = 2x + 4, giving y = 2x + 9. Verify: (−1/2)(2) = −1. Correct!

lessons.tip: To quickly check if two slopes are perpendicular, multiply them — if the product is −1, the lines are perpendicular. For parallel lines, simply compare: the slopes must be exactly equal.

quiz.q: A line has slope 3/5. What is the slope of a line perpendicular to it?
quiz.explanation: The negative reciprocal of 3/5 is −5/3. Flip the fraction and change the sign.

quiz.q: Which of the following lines is parallel to y = 4x − 3?
quiz.explanation: Parallel lines have the same slope. y = 4x + 7 has the same slope of 4 as y = 4x − 3, but a different y-intercept.

quiz.q: Two perpendicular lines have slopes m and n. Which equation must be true?
quiz.explanation: Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, so their product m × n = −1.

lessons.title: Coordinate Proofs
lessons.description: Prove theorems using coordinate geometry.
vocabulary: Coordinate proof — a proof that uses the coordinate plane and distance, midpoint, and slope formulas
Distance formula — d = √[(x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²], derived from the Pythagorean theorem
Midpoint formula — M = ((x₁+x₂)/2, (y₁+y₂)/2), finds the center of a segment
Slope formula — m = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁), used to prove parallelism and perpendicularity
Vertex placement — the strategy of placing figures at convenient coordinates to simplify calculations
Variable coordinates — using variables like (a, b) to represent general positions on the coordinate plane
lessons.formula:
Distance formula: d = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²]
Midpoint formula: M = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2)
Slope formula: m = (y₂ − y₁)/(x₂ − x₁)

Parallel: same slope | Perpendicular: m₁ × m₂ = −1
lessons.content:
A coordinate proof uses the coordinate plane to prove geometric properties algebraically. Instead of relying on traditional deductive reasoning with theorems and postulates, you assign coordinates to vertices and use the distance formula, midpoint formula, and slope formula to verify geometric relationships. This method is especially powerful for proving that triangles are congruent, isosceles, or right-angled.

The key to an efficient coordinate proof is strategic placement. Place one vertex at the origin (0, 0) and another on the x-axis or y-axis. This reduces the number of variables and simplifies all calculations. For instance, to prove a triangle is isosceles, you only need to show two sides have equal length using the distance formula. To prove a right angle, show two sides have slopes that are negative reciprocals (product = −1).

Coordinate proofs combine algebra with geometry, so organization is critical. Clearly state your coordinate assignments, show each formula substitution step, and conclude by connecting the algebraic result back to the geometric claim. Common proof targets include proving a quadrilateral is a parallelogram (show both pairs of opposite sides are parallel via equal slopes) or a rectangle (show all angles are right angles).
steps: Place the figure on the coordinate plane strategically: put one vertex at the origin and another on an axis
Assign coordinates to all vertices, using variables when needed
Identify what you need to prove (congruent sides, right angle, parallel sides, etc.)
Apply the appropriate formula: distance for lengths, slope for parallel/perpendicular, midpoint for bisectors
Perform the algebraic calculations step by step
State the conclusion: connect the computed result to the geometric property being proved

examples.title: Proving a Triangle Is Isosceles
examples.text: Prove that triangle ABC with vertices A(0, 0), B(4, 0), and C(2, 6) is isosceles. Find AB = √[(4−0)² + (0−0)²] = 4. Find AC = √[(2−0)² + (6−0)²] = √(4 + 36) = √40. Find BC = √[(2−4)² + (6−0)²] = √(4 + 36) = √40. Since AC = BC = √40, two sides are equal, so triangle ABC is isosceles with AC = BC.

examples.title: Proving a Right Angle Using Slope
examples.text: Prove that triangle with vertices P(0, 0), Q(6, 0), and R(0, 8) has a right angle at P. Find slope of PQ: (0 − 0)/(6 − 0) = 0 (horizontal). Find slope of PR: (8 − 0)/(0 − 0) = undefined (vertical). A horizontal line is perpendicular to a vertical line, so angle P is a right angle (90°). Therefore, triangle PQR is a right triangle.

lessons.tip: Always place your figure to minimize variables. Put one vertex at the origin and another on the x-axis. This halves your workload and reduces algebraic errors. The fewer variables you track, the cleaner your proof.

quiz.q: What formula would you use to prove two segments have equal length in a coordinate proof?
quiz.explanation: The distance formula calculates the length of a segment between two points, so it is used to compare lengths and prove segments are congruent.

quiz.q: In a coordinate proof, where should you place the first vertex of your figure?
options: At the center of the plane
quiz.explanation: Placing a vertex at the origin (0, 0) simplifies calculations because coordinates become zero, reducing the complexity of all formulas.

quiz.q: To prove two lines in a coordinate proof are perpendicular, you would show that:
quiz.explanation: Perpendicular lines have slopes that are negative reciprocals, meaning their product equals −1.

lessons.title: Translations
lessons.description: Slide figures without turning them.
vocabulary: Translation — a rigid transformation that slides every point of a figure the same distance and direction
Vector — an ordered pair (a, b) that describes the horizontal and vertical shift of a translation
Pre-image — the original figure before a transformation is applied
Image — the resulting figure after a transformation is applied
Rigid motion — a transformation that preserves size and shape (distance and angle measure)
Component form — writing a translation as (x, y) → (x + h, y + k), where h and k are shift amounts
Congruent — figures that have the same size and shape after a rigid transformation
lessons.formula:
Translation rule: (x, y) → (x + h, y + k)

h = horizontal shift (positive = right, negative = left)
k = vertical shift (positive = up, negative = down)

Vector notation: ⟨h, k⟩
Distance preserved: d(P', Q') = d(P, Q)
lessons.content:
A translation (or slide) moves every point of a figure the same distance in the same direction. It is described by the rule (x, y) → (x + h, y + k), where h represents the horizontal shift and k represents the vertical shift. Translations are rigid motions, meaning they preserve the size and shape of the figure — the image is always congruent to the pre-image.

To perform a translation, add h to every x-coordinate and add k to every y-coordinate of the figure's vertices. For example, a translation with rule (x, y) → (x + 3, y − 2) shifts every point 3 units right and 2 units down. A positive h shifts right, a negative h shifts left, a positive k shifts up, and a negative k shifts down. You can also describe a translation as a vector ⟨h, k⟩ drawn from any point to its image.

Translations have several important properties: all corresponding line segments remain equal in length, all corresponding angles remain equal in measure, and the orientation of the figure is preserved (it is not flipped or rotated). To find the translation rule when given a pre-image and image, simply subtract the coordinates of any corresponding pair of points to find h and k.
steps: Identify the translation rule (x, y) → (x + h, y + k) or the vector ⟨h, k⟩
List the coordinates of each vertex of the pre-image
Apply the rule to each vertex: add h to x and add k to y
Plot the new image vertices on the coordinate plane
Connect the vertices in the same order as the original figure
Verify the image is congruent to the pre-image by comparing side lengths

examples.title: Translating a Triangle
examples.text: Translate triangle ABC with vertices A(1, 2), B(4, 3), and C(2, 5) using the rule (x, y) → (x − 3, y + 4). Apply the rule to each vertex: A' = (1 − 3, 2 + 4) = (−2, 6), B' = (4 − 3, 3 + 4) = (1, 7), C' = (2 − 3, 5 + 4) = (−1, 9). The image triangle A'B'C' is congruent to ABC but shifted 3 units left and 4 units up.

examples.title: Finding the Translation Rule
examples.text: Point P(3, 5) is translated to P'(7, 1). Find the translation rule. Since (x, y) → (x + h, y + k), we have 3 + h = 7 and 5 + k = 1. Solving: h = 4 and k = −4. The translation rule is (x, y) → (x + 4, y − 4), or vector ⟨4, −4⟩. This means every point shifts 4 units right and 4 units down.

lessons.tip: When finding an unknown translation rule, subtract the pre-image coordinates from the image coordinates: h = x' − x and k = y' − y. This works for any corresponding point pair.

quiz.q: Under the translation (x, y) → (x + 5, y − 3), where does point (2, 7) map to?
quiz.explanation: Apply the rule: x' = 2 + 5 = 7, y' = 7 − 3 = 4. The image point is (7, 4).

quiz.q: Which of the following is true about a translation?
options: It changes the size of the figure
It preserves the shape and size of the figure
It flips the figure across a line
quiz.explanation: A translation is a rigid motion that slides a figure without changing its size, shape, or orientation. The image is always congruent to the pre-image.

quiz.q: If point A(4, −1) maps to A'(1, 3) under a translation, what is the vector for this translation?

lessons.title: Reflections
lessons.description: Flip figures across a line.
vocabulary: Reflection — a rigid transformation that flips a figure across a line of reflection
Line of reflection — the line across which a figure is reflected (mirror line)
X-axis reflection rule — (x, y) → (x, −y); the y-coordinate changes sign
Y-axis reflection rule — (x, y) → (−x, y); the x-coordinate changes sign
Line y = x reflection rule — (x, y) → (y, x); the coordinates swap positions
Line of symmetry — a line that divides a figure into two mirror-image halves
Orientation — the order of vertices; reflections reverse orientation (clockwise becomes counterclockwise)
lessons.formula:
Reflection across x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y)
Reflection across y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y)
Reflection across y = x: (x, y) → (y, x)
Reflection across y = −x: (x, y) → (−y, −x)
Reflection across x = a: (x, y) → (2a − x, y)
Reflection across y = b: (x, y) → (x, 2b − y)
lessons.content:
A reflection flips a figure across a line called the line of reflection, creating a mirror image. Each point of the original figure and its image are the same distance from the line of reflection, and the line connecting each point to its image is perpendicular to the line of reflection. Like translations, reflections are rigid motions that preserve distance and angle measure.

There are standard rules for reflecting across common lines. Reflecting across the x-axis changes the sign of the y-coordinate: (x, y) → (x, −y). Reflecting across the y-axis changes the sign of the x-coordinate: (x, y) → (−x, y). Reflecting across the line y = x swaps the coordinates: (x, y) → (y, x). For reflection across vertical line x = a, use (x, y) → (2a − x, y); for horizontal line y = b, use (x, y) → (x, 2b − y).

Unlike translations, reflections reverse the orientation of a figure. If the vertices of the pre-image are listed clockwise, the image vertices will be listed counterclockwise. This is an important distinction: both translations and reflections produce congruent images, but only reflections change the direction of orientation. Recognizing this helps when identifying which transformation was applied.
steps: Identify the line of reflection
Write down the correct reflection rule for that line
List the coordinates of each vertex of the pre-image
Apply the rule to each vertex to find the image coordinates
Plot the image and verify each point is the same distance from the line as its pre-image
Check that orientation is reversed (clockwise becomes counterclockwise)

examples.title: Reflecting Across the X-axis
examples.text: Reflect triangle ABC with vertices A(2, 5), B(4, 1), and C(1, 3) across the x-axis. The rule is (x, y) → (x, −y). Apply to each vertex: A' = (2, −5), B' = (4, −1), C' = (1, −3). Notice that point (2, 5) is 5 units above the x-axis and its image (2, −5) is 5 units below — equal distances from the mirror line. The triangle A'B'C' is congruent to ABC but flipped.

examples.title: Reflecting Across the Line y = x
examples.text: Reflect point P(3, 7) across the line y = x. The rule is (x, y) → (y, x), so P' = (7, 3). You can verify: the midpoint of P and P' is ((3+7)/2, (7+3)/2) = (5, 5), which lies on the line y = x. The line PP' has slope (3−7)/(7−3) = −1, which is perpendicular to y = x (slope 1). This confirms the reflection is correct.

lessons.tip: To quickly remember reflection rules: reflecting across the x-axis flips the y-value (top to bottom), reflecting across the y-axis flips the x-value (left to right), and reflecting across y = x swaps the coordinates entirely.

quiz.q: What is the image of (3, −4) after a reflection across the y-axis?
quiz.explanation: Reflection across the y-axis changes the sign of x: (x, y) → (−x, y). So (3, −4) → (−3, −4).

quiz.q: Under a reflection across the line y = x, what happens to the coordinates?
options: The x- and y-coordinates swap places
quiz.explanation: Reflection across y = x swaps coordinates: (x, y) → (y, x).

quiz.q: How does a reflection affect the orientation of a figure?
options: It has no effect on orientation
quiz.explanation: Reflections reverse the orientation of a figure. If vertices are listed clockwise in the pre-image, they will be counterclockwise in the image.

lessons.title: Rotations
lessons.description: Turn figures around a fixed point.
vocabulary: Rotation — a rigid transformation that turns a figure about a fixed point called the center of rotation
Center of rotation — the fixed point about which a figure is rotated
Angle of rotation — the degree measure and direction (clockwise or counterclockwise) of the turn
Rotational symmetry — a figure can be mapped onto itself by a rotation less than 360°
Counterclockwise (CCW) — the positive direction of rotation
Clockwise (CW) — the negative direction of rotation
Order of rotational symmetry — the number of times a figure maps onto itself during a 360° rotation
lessons.formula:
Rotation 90° CCW about origin: (x, y) → (−y, x)
Rotation 180° about origin: (x, y) → (−x, −y)
Rotation 270° CCW about origin: (x, y) → (y, −x)

90° CW = 270° CCW: (x, y) → (y, −x)
180° is its own inverse: applying twice returns to (x, y)
Distance from center is preserved: d(P, center) = d(P', center)
lessons.content:
A rotation turns a figure around a fixed point called the center of rotation by a specified angle. In most coordinate geometry problems, rotations are performed about the origin (0, 0). Rotations are rigid motions — they preserve the size and shape of the figure. The distance from every point to the center of rotation stays the same.

There are standard rotation rules for common angles about the origin. A 90° counterclockwise rotation maps (x, y) to (−y, x). A 180° rotation maps (x, y) to (−x, −y). A 270° counterclockwise rotation (which is the same as 90° clockwise) maps (x, y) to (y, −x). A useful pattern: each additional 90° CCW rotation swaps the coordinates and adjusts the signs in a predictable cycle.

Some figures have rotational symmetry, meaning they look the same after a rotation of less than 360°. A regular n-gon has rotational symmetry of order n (it maps onto itself every 360°/n degrees). A rectangle has rotational symmetry of order 2 (180°), while an equilateral triangle has order 3 (120°). Identifying rotational symmetry helps understand the structure of geometric figures.
steps: Identify the center of rotation and the angle of rotation
Determine the correct rotation rule for the given angle
List the coordinates of each vertex of the pre-image
Apply the rotation rule to each vertex
Plot the rotated image and verify distances from the center are preserved
Check that the angle between corresponding segments equals the rotation angle

examples.title: Rotating a Triangle 90° Counterclockwise
examples.text: Rotate triangle ABC with A(2, 1), B(5, 3), and C(1, 4) by 90° CCW about the origin. Using the rule (x, y) → (−y, x): A' = (−1, 2), B' = (−3, 5), C' = (−4, 1). Verify: the distance from A(2, 1) to origin is √(4+1) = √5, and from A'(−1, 2) to origin is √(1+4) = √5. Distances are preserved, confirming a correct rotation.

examples.title: Rotating 180° About the Origin
examples.text: Rotate quadrilateral PQRS with P(3, 2), Q(7, 2), R(8, 5), and S(2, 6) by 180° about the origin. The 180° rule is (x, y) → (−x, −y). Apply to each: P' = (−3, −2), Q' = (−7, −2), R' = (−8, −5), S' = (−2, −6). A 180° rotation is equivalent to two 90° rotations and is its own inverse — rotating again by 180° brings the figure back to its original position.

lessons.tip: To remember the 90° CCW rule (−y, x), think of a clock: the x-axis 'rotates up' to become the y-axis, so the old y-value goes to the negative x-position and the old x-value goes to the positive y-position.

quiz.q: What is the image of point (3, −5) after a 90° counterclockwise rotation about the origin?
A 180° rotation about the origin maps (x, y) to:
quiz.explanation: A 180° rotation negates both coordinates: (x, y) → (−x, −y). It is like reflecting across both axes simultaneously.

quiz.q: A regular hexagon has rotational symmetry of what order?
quiz.explanation: A regular hexagon (6 sides) has rotational symmetry of order 6. It maps onto itself every 360°/6 = 60° of rotation.

lessons.title: Dilations
lessons.description: Resize figures by a scale factor.
vocabulary: Dilation — a transformation that enlarges or reduces a figure by a scale factor about a center point
Scale factor (k) — the ratio by which all distances from the center are multiplied; k > 1 enlarges, 0 < k < 1 reduces
Center of dilation — the fixed point from which all distances are scaled
Similarity transformation — a transformation that produces a similar (same shape, possibly different size) image
Enlargement — a dilation with scale factor k > 1, producing a larger image
Reduction — a dilation with scale factor 0 < k < 1, producing a smaller image
Congruent — figures with k = 1 are congruent (same size and shape)
lessons.formula:
Dilation about origin: (x, y) → (kx, ky)
Dilation about point (a, b): (x, y) → (a + k(x−a), b + k(y−b))

Scale factor k = image length / pre-image length
Enlargement: k > 1
Reduction: 0 < k < 1
k = 1: congruent (no size change)
Angle measures are preserved
lessons.content:
A dilation is a transformation that changes the size of a figure by multiplying all distances from a center point by a scale factor k. Unlike rigid motions (translations, reflections, rotations), dilations change the size of the figure but preserve the shape — the image is always similar to the pre-image. All angle measures remain the same, and all corresponding sides are proportional.

When the center of dilation is the origin, the rule is simple: (x, y) → (kx, ky). Multiply each coordinate by k. A scale factor greater than 1 produces an enlargement, while a scale factor between 0 and 1 produces a reduction. A negative scale factor both dilates and rotates the figure 180° about the center. To find the scale factor, compare any pair of corresponding side lengths: k = image length / pre-image length.

Dilations are the basis of similarity transformations. Any two similar figures can be related by a sequence of rigid motions followed by a dilation. The scale factor tells you the ratio of all corresponding lengths, areas (k²), and volumes (k³). Understanding dilations is essential for working with similar triangles, scale drawings, maps, and models.
steps: Identify the center of dilation and the scale factor k
For dilation about the origin, multiply each coordinate by k: (x, y) → (kx, ky)
For dilation about another point (a, b), apply: (x, y) → (a + k(x−a), b + k(y−b))
Calculate the new coordinates for each vertex
Verify that corresponding side lengths have the ratio k
Confirm that all angle measures are unchanged (dilation preserves angles)

examples.title: Dilating a Triangle About the Origin
examples.text: Dilate triangle DEF with D(2, 4), E(6, 2), and F(4, 8) by a scale factor of k = 1.5 about the origin. Multiply each coordinate by 1.5: D' = (3, 6), E' = (9, 3), F' = (6, 12). Verify: side DE has length √[(6−2)² + (2−4)²] = √(16+4) = √20. Side D'E' has length √[(9−3)² + (3−6)²] = √(36+9) = √45 = 1.5√20. The ratio is 1.5 = k. Correct!

examples.title: Finding the Scale Factor
examples.text: Triangle GHI has GH = 8. After a dilation, the image G'H'I' has G'H' = 12. Find the scale factor. k = G'H' / GH = 12 / 8 = 1.5. Since k > 1, this is an enlargement. All other corresponding sides are also multiplied by 1.5, and the area of G'H'I' is (1.5)² = 2.25 times the area of GHI.

lessons.tip: The scale factor affects different measures differently: lengths multiply by k, areas multiply by k², and volumes multiply by k³. Keep track of which measure you are comparing to use the correct power of k.

quiz.q: Under a dilation with scale factor k = 2 about the origin, what is the image of (3, −4)?
quiz.explanation: Multiply each coordinate by k = 2: (2×3, 2×(−4)) = (6, −8).

quiz.q: A dilation with scale factor k = 0.5 produces what kind of image?
options: An enlargement twice the original size
A reduction half the original size
quiz.explanation: A scale factor of 0.5 (between 0 and 1) produces a reduction. Each dimension becomes half of the original, so the image is smaller.

quiz.q: Which of the following is preserved under a dilation?
quiz.explanation: Dilations preserve angle measures. The shape stays the same while side lengths, perimeter, and area all change proportionally to k, k, and k² respectively.

lessons.title: Composite Transformations
lessons.description: Combine multiple transformations.
vocabulary: Composite transformation — two or more transformations performed in sequence on a figure
Glide reflection — a translation followed by a reflection across a line parallel to the translation
Transformation order — the sequence in which transformations are applied; order usually matters
Composition — the result of applying one transformation after another
Pre-image — the original figure before any transformations
Final image — the figure after all transformations have been applied
Equivalent transformation — a single transformation that produces the same result as a composition
lessons.formula:
Composition notation: R₂ ∘ R₁ means apply R₁ first, then R₂

Common compositions:
Two reflections across parallel lines = translation
Two reflections across intersecting lines = rotation
Glide reflection = translation + reflection (parallel)

Note: Order matters in most cases!
lessons.content:
A composite transformation is a sequence of two or more transformations applied one after another. The result of applying transformation B after transformation A is written as B ∘ A, meaning 'do A first, then B.' In most cases, order matters — rotating 90° then reflecting across the x-axis gives a different result than reflecting across the x-axis then rotating 90°.

Some compositions are equivalent to a single transformation. Two reflections across parallel lines are equivalent to a translation whose distance is twice the distance between the lines. Two reflections across intersecting lines are equivalent to a rotation about the intersection point by twice the angle between the lines. These equivalences are powerful shortcuts that simplify complex problems.

A special type of composition called a glide reflection combines a translation with a reflection across a line parallel to the translation direction. For example, translate 3 units right, then reflect across a horizontal line. Glide reflections are one of only four types of isometries (along with translations, reflections, and rotations). When solving composite transformation problems, work step by step: apply the first transformation, then use the result as the pre-image for the second.
steps: Identify the sequence of transformations and the order in which they must be applied
Apply the first transformation to all vertices of the pre-image
Use the resulting coordinates as the pre-image for the second transformation
Apply the second transformation to get the final image coordinates
Plot the final image and verify each step is correct
If possible, identify a single equivalent transformation for the entire composition

examples.title: Rotation Then Reflection
examples.text: Apply a 90° CCW rotation about the origin followed by a reflection across the x-axis to point (3, 2). Step 1 — Rotate 90° CCW: (3, 2) → (−2, 3). Step 2 — Reflect across x-axis: (−2, 3) → (−2, −3). The final image is (−2, −3). Compare with the reverse order: reflect first (−3, 2), then rotate 90° CCW (−2, −3). In this case, the result is the same, but this is not always true!

examples.title: Glide Reflection
examples.text: Perform a glide reflection on triangle with vertex (1, 4) using translation (x, y) → (x + 3, y) followed by reflection across the x-axis. Step 1 — Translate: (1, 4) → (4, 4). Step 2 — Reflect across x-axis: (4, 4) → (4, −4). The glide reflection maps (1, 4) to (4, −4). The translation moves the point right and the reflection flips it below the axis.

lessons.tip: When working through composite transformations, apply one transformation at a time and keep track of coordinates at each step. A small mistake in an early step will carry through and make the final answer wrong. Organize your work in a table with columns for each step.

quiz.q: Two reflections across parallel lines are equivalent to which single transformation?
quiz.explanation: Two reflections across parallel lines produce a translation. The translation distance equals twice the distance between the two parallel lines.

quiz.q: In a composite transformation, does the order of transformations matter?
options: Yes, order matters in most cases
quiz.explanation: In most cases, the order of transformations matters. Rotating then reflecting usually gives a different result than reflecting then rotating.

quiz.q: A glide reflection consists of:
options: A rotation followed by a dilation
A translation followed by a reflection across a parallel line
Two reflections across the same line
quiz.explanation: A glide reflection is a translation followed by a reflection across a line parallel to the direction of translation.

lessons.title: Basic Area Formulas
lessons.description: Calculate areas of rectangles, triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids.
vocabulary: Area — the number of square units needed to cover a two-dimensional figure
Base — the side of a figure used as the reference for calculating area
Height (altitude) — the perpendicular distance from the base to the opposite side or vertex
Rectangle — a quadrilateral with four right angles; area = base × height
Parallelogram — a quadrilateral with opposite sides parallel; area = base × height
Trapezoid — a quadrilateral with exactly one pair of parallel sides (bases)
Square units — the units used to measure area (cm², m², ft², etc.)
lessons.formula:
Rectangle: A = l × w
Parallelogram: A = b × h
Triangle: A = ½bh
Trapezoid: A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h
Square: A = s²
Rhombus/Kite: A = ½d₁d₂

b = base, h = height (altitude)
d = diagonal
lessons.content:
Area formulas allow you to calculate the amount of space inside two-dimensional shapes. The most fundamental formula is the rectangle: A = length × width. From this, the parallelogram formula follows directly (A = base × height) because a parallelogram can be transformed into a rectangle with the same base and height. The triangle formula A = ½bh makes sense because any triangle is exactly half of a parallelogram with the same base and height.

The trapezoid requires both parallel sides (bases): A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h. This formula averages the two bases and multiplies by the height. A helpful way to remember it: a trapezoid is the average of two parallelograms stacked together. For special quadrilaterals, a rhombus or kite uses A = ½d₁d₂, where d₁ and d₂ are the lengths of the diagonals.

A critical concept is understanding the height (altitude) of a figure. The height must always be perpendicular to the base. In a parallelogram, the height is not necessarily a side — it is the perpendicular distance between the parallel sides. When a problem gives you a slanted side length instead of a height, you may need to use the Pythagorean theorem or trigonometry to find the actual perpendicular height before applying the area formula.
steps: Identify the shape and the correct area formula to use
Locate the base(s) and the perpendicular height in the given information
If the height is not given directly, use trigonometry or the Pythagorean theorem to find it
Substitute the values into the formula and compute the area
Include the correct square units in your answer
For composite shapes, break them into familiar shapes, find individual areas, then add or subtract

examples.title: Area of a Trapezoid
examples.text: Find the area of a trapezoid with bases of 10 cm and 14 cm and a height of 6 cm. Using A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h: A = ½(10 + 14)(6) = ½(24)(6) = 12 × 6 = 72 cm². The average of the bases is (10 + 14)/2 = 12, and multiplied by the height of 6 gives 72 square centimeters.

examples.title: Finding Height of a Parallelogram
examples.text: A parallelogram has a base of 15 cm, a side of 13 cm, and an area of 120 cm². Find the height. Using A = bh: 120 = 15 × h, so h = 120/15 = 8 cm. The perpendicular height is 8 cm. Note: the side length of 13 cm is not used in the area calculation — the height is the perpendicular distance, not the slanted side.

lessons.tip: The height in an area formula must be perpendicular to the base. If you are given a slanted side length instead of the height, draw the altitude and use the Pythagorean theorem or trig ratios to find the perpendicular height first.

quiz.q: What is the area of a triangle with base 12 cm and height 7 cm?
A trapezoid has bases of 8 and 12 meters and a height of 5 meters. What is its area?
Why is the triangle area formula ½bh instead of bh?
options: Because a triangle is half of a parallelogram with the same base and height
Because triangles are smaller than rectangles
Because the base of a triangle is curved
quiz.explanation: A triangle is exactly half of a parallelogram with the same base and height. Since the parallelogram area is bh, the triangle area is ½bh.

lessons.title: Complex Figures
lessons.description: Find areas of composite and irregular shapes.
vocabulary: Composite figure — a shape made up of two or more basic geometric shapes combined
Decomposition — breaking a complex figure into simpler shapes to calculate area
Subtraction method — finding the area of an outer shape and subtracting the area of a cutout region
Addition method — splitting a complex figure into parts, finding each area, and adding them together
Irregular shape — a figure that does not match a standard geometric shape formula
Apex — the top vertex of a figure such as a triangle or pyramid
Overlapping regions — areas where two shapes share space, requiring subtraction to avoid double-counting
lessons.formula:
Composite Area = Σ (areas of individual parts)

Subtraction method:
Area = Area(outer shape) − Area(cutout)

Addition method:
Area = Area(part 1) + Area(part 2) + Area(part 3) + ...

Shaded area: Area(whole) − Area(unshaded)
lessons.content:
Many real-world shapes are composite figures made up of rectangles, triangles, circles, and other basic shapes combined. To find the area of a composite figure, you use one of two strategies: decomposition (breaking the figure into familiar parts and adding their areas) or the subtraction method (finding the area of a larger enclosing shape and subtracting the area of a removed region).

The decomposition (addition) method works best when a figure can be naturally divided into rectangles, triangles, trapezoids, or semicircles. Draw dashed lines to separate the figure into parts, calculate each area using standard formulas, and add them together. The subtraction method is ideal for shapes with holes or cutouts, such as a rectangular region with a circular cutout, or a walkway around a garden.

For shaded area problems, the key formula is: shaded area = total area − unshaded area. Read the problem carefully to determine whether you need to add or subtract. Sometimes both methods are needed in the same problem. Always label each region clearly, show all calculations, and include units throughout your work to avoid errors.
steps: Visualize the figure and identify the basic shapes that compose it
Choose a strategy: decomposition (add parts) or subtraction (outer minus cutout)
If decomposing, draw dashed lines to separate the figure into recognizable shapes
Calculate the area of each part using the appropriate formula
Add all part areas (decomposition) or subtract the cutout from the outer shape (subtraction)
State the final answer with correct square units

examples.title: Area of an L-Shaped Figure
examples.text: Find the area of an L-shaped figure that can be split into a 10 cm × 4 cm rectangle on top and an 4 cm × 6 cm rectangle on the side. Using decomposition: Area = (10 × 4) + (4 × 6) = 40 + 24 = 64 cm². Alternatively, enclose the L-shape in a 10 cm × 10 cm square and subtract the 6 cm × 6 cm cutout: Area = (10 × 10) − (6 × 6) = 100 − 36 = 64 cm². Both methods give the same result.

examples.title: Shaded Area in a Circle
examples.text: A circle of radius 10 cm has a square inscribed inside it. Find the area of the shaded region (the part of the circle outside the square). The circle area is π(10)² = 100π ≈ 314.16 cm². The diagonal of the square equals the diameter of the circle (20 cm), so the side of the square is 20/√2 = 10√2 cm. Square area = (10√2)² = 200 cm². Shaded area = 100π − 200 ≈ 114.16 cm².

lessons.tip: When a composite figure has a regular outer boundary with an irregular cutout, the subtraction method is often faster than decomposition. Enclose the figure in a large regular shape and subtract the cutout area.

quiz.q: A figure is made of a semicircle (r = 5 cm) on top of a rectangle (10 cm × 6 cm). What is the total area?
quiz.explanation: Rectangle area = 10 × 6 = 60 cm². Semicircle area = ½π(5)² = 12.5π cm². Total = 60 + 12.5π cm².

quiz.q: The subtraction method for composite figures involves:
options: Finding the area of the outer shape and subtracting the cutout
Dividing the shape into triangles only
quiz.explanation: The subtraction method calculates the area of the outer enclosing shape and subtracts the area of the removed (cutout) region.

quiz.q: A 12 m × 8 m rectangular garden has a 4 m × 4 m square shed in one corner. What is the garden area excluding the shed?
quiz.explanation: Total rectangle area = 12 × 8 = 96 m². Shed area = 4 × 4 = 16 m². Garden excluding shed = 96 − 16 = 80 m².

lessons.title: Circles: Circumference and Area
lessons.description: Calculate circumference and area of circles.
vocabulary: Circle — the set of all points equidistant from a fixed center point
Radius (r) — the distance from the center to any point on the circle
Diameter (d) — the distance across the circle through the center; d = 2r
Circumference (C) — the distance around the circle (perimeter of a circle)
Pi (π) — the ratio of circumference to diameter; approximately 3.14159
Area (A) — the number of square units inside the circle
Semicircle — exactly half of a circle; area = πr²/2, arc length = πr
lessons.formula:
Circumference: C = 2πr = πd
Area: A = πr²

Semicircle area: A = πr²/2
Semicircle perimeter: P = πr + 2r (arc + diameter)

r = C/(2π) = d/2
d = C/π = 2r
Use π ≈ 3.14 or leave in terms of π
lessons.content:
A circle is defined by all points that are the same distance (the radius) from a center point. The distance around a circle is called the circumference, and it is calculated using C = 2πr or C = πd. The constant π (pi) represents the ratio of any circle's circumference to its diameter and is approximately 3.14159. In exact answers, leave π as a symbol; for decimal answers, use 3.14 or your calculator's π button.

The area of a circle is A = πr². Notice that the area formula uses the radius squared, not the diameter. A common mistake is to use d² instead of r², or to double the area when working with diameter. If you are given the diameter, always halve it first to get the radius. For problems involving semicircles, remember to use half the area (πr²/2) and include the diameter when calculating perimeter.

Circle problems often involve multiple steps. You may need to find the radius from the circumference first (r = C/2π), then use that radius to find the area. For shaded region problems, subtract the area of an inner circle from an outer circle: shaded area = π(R² − r²), where R is the outer radius and r is the inner radius. This is called the area of an annulus (ring-shaped region).
steps: Identify what is given: radius, diameter, circumference, or area
If given the diameter, convert to radius by dividing by 2
If given circumference, solve for radius: r = C/(2π)
Apply the appropriate formula: C = 2πr for circumference or A = πr² for area
For semicircles, halve the area and remember to include the diameter in perimeter calculations
Round appropriately or leave the answer in terms of π as directed

examples.title: Finding Area from Circumference
examples.text: A circle has a circumference of 31.4 cm. Find its area. First, find the radius: r = C/(2π) = 31.4/(2 × 3.14) = 5 cm. Now find the area: A = πr² = 3.14 × 5² = 3.14 × 25 = 78.5 cm². Always find the radius before applying the area formula.

examples.title: Area of an Annulus (Ring)
examples.text: A circular garden has an outer radius of 10 m and an inner radius (fountain) of 3 m. Find the area of the garden around the fountain. Outer area = π(10)² = 100π m². Inner area = π(3)² = 9π m². Garden area = 100π − 9π = 91π ≈ 285.88 m². The shaded ring area formula is π(R² − r²).

lessons.tip: When given the diameter, always divide by 2 to get the radius before using any formula. The area formula uses r² (not d²), and the circumference formula C = πd uses d directly but C = 2πr uses r.

quiz.q: What is the area of a circle with radius 7 cm? (Leave in terms of π)
quiz.explanation: A = πr² = π(7)² = 49π cm².

quiz.q: A circle has circumference 20π cm. What is its radius?
quiz.explanation: C = 2πr, so 20π = 2πr. Divide both sides by 2π: r = 10 cm.

quiz.q: What is the area of a semicircle with radius 6 inches? (Leave in terms of π)
quiz.explanation: Semicircle area = ½πr² = ½π(6)² = ½(36π) = 18π in².

lessons.title: Prisms
lessons.description: Find surface area and volume of prisms.
vocabulary: Prism — a 3D solid with two parallel congruent polygonal bases and rectangular lateral faces
Lateral surface area — the total area of the sides (faces) excluding the bases
Total surface area — the sum of the lateral area and the areas of both bases
Volume — the amount of space inside a solid, measured in cubic units
Base area (B) — the area of one of the congruent polygonal bases
Height (h) — the perpendicular distance between the two bases
Lateral edge — the edge connecting corresponding vertices of the two bases; perpendicular to bases in a right prism
lessons.formula:
Volume: V = Bh

Lateral Surface Area: L = Ph
  (P = perimeter of base, h = height)

Total Surface Area: S = L + 2B = Ph + 2B

Rectangular prism: V = lwh
  S = 2(lw + lh + wh)

B = area of one base
h = height of the prism
lessons.content:
A prism is a three-dimensional solid with two parallel, congruent bases connected by rectangular lateral faces. The most common type is the rectangular prism (box shape), but prisms can have triangular, pentagonal, hexagonal, or any polygonal base. The key principle for all prisms is that the volume equals the base area times the height: V = Bh.

The lateral surface area of a prism is the area of only the side faces (not the bases). For any prism, the lateral area equals the perimeter of the base times the height: L = Ph. The total surface area adds the areas of both bases: S = Ph + 2B. For a rectangular prism specifically, the total surface area is S = 2(lw + lh + wh), and the volume is V = lwh.

When solving prism problems, first identify the shape of the base to determine which area formula to use for B. For a triangular prism, you need the triangle area formula (½bh). For a hexagonal prism, you need the hexagon area formula. The height h of the prism is always the perpendicular distance between the two bases. Be careful not to confuse the base edge lengths with the prism height — they are different measurements.
steps: Identify the shape of the base and find its area B using the appropriate 2D formula
Find the perimeter P of the base
Identify the height h of the prism (perpendicular distance between bases)
Calculate volume: V = Bh
Calculate lateral surface area: L = Ph
Calculate total surface area: S = Ph + 2B (or S = L + 2B)

examples.title: Triangular Prism Volume and Surface Area
examples.text: Find the volume and total surface area of a triangular prism with a triangular base of base 6 cm, height 4 cm, and prism height 10 cm. Base area B = ½(6)(4) = 12 cm². Base perimeter P = 6 + 5 + 5 = 16 cm (assuming isosceles). Volume V = Bh = 12 × 10 = 120 cm³. Lateral area L = Ph = 16 × 10 = 160 cm². Total surface area S = 160 + 2(12) = 184 cm².

examples.title: Rectangular Prism
examples.text: A rectangular box has length 8 cm, width 5 cm, and height 12 cm. Find volume and total surface area. Volume V = lwh = 8 × 5 × 12 = 480 cm³. Surface area S = 2(lw + lh + wh) = 2(40 + 96 + 60) = 2(196) = 392 cm². This formula accounts for all six rectangular faces of the box.

lessons.tip: For all prisms, the volume formula V = Bh works universally. Just remember that B is the area of the base (use whichever 2D formula matches the base shape), and h is the height of the prism (distance between the two parallel bases).

quiz.q: A rectangular prism has dimensions 3, 4, and 5. What is its volume?
quiz.explanation: V = lwh = 3 × 4 × 5 = 60 cubic units.

quiz.q: The lateral surface area of a prism is calculated using which formula?
quiz.explanation: The lateral surface area of any prism is L = Ph, where P is the perimeter of the base and h is the prism height.

quiz.q: A triangular prism has a base area of 15 cm² and a height of 8 cm. What is its volume?
quiz.explanation: V = Bh = 15 × 8 = 120 cm³. The base area B = 15 and prism height h = 8.

lessons.title: Cylinders
lessons.description: Calculate surface area and volume of cylinders.
vocabulary: Cylinder — a 3D solid with two parallel congruent circular bases connected by a curved surface
Lateral area — the area of the curved side of the cylinder, which unrolls into a rectangle
Total surface area — the lateral area plus the areas of both circular bases
Radius (r) — the distance from the center of a circular base to its edge
Height (h) — the perpendicular distance between the two circular bases
Base area — the area of one circular base: B = πr²
Net — the 2D pattern formed by 'unrolling' a cylinder: a rectangle plus two circles
lessons.formula:
Volume: V = πr²h

Lateral Surface Area: L = 2πrh
  (circumference × height)

Total Surface Area: S = 2πr(r + h)
  = 2πr² + 2πrh
  = 2B + L

r = radius, h = height
B = πr² (area of one base)
lessons.content:
A cylinder is a three-dimensional solid with two parallel, congruent circular bases and a curved lateral surface. Think of it as a stack of infinitely thin circles. Cylinders are everywhere in daily life: cans, pipes, water tanks, and columns are all cylindrical shapes. The key measurements are the radius r (of the circular base) and the height h (distance between the bases).

The volume of a cylinder is V = πr²h, which is the area of the circular base times the height. This matches the general prism formula V = Bh where B = πr². The lateral surface area is L = 2πrh, which equals the circumference of the base (2πr) times the height — if you 'unroll' the curved surface, it forms a rectangle with these dimensions. The total surface area adds both circular bases: S = 2πr² + 2πrh = 2πr(r + h).

When solving cylinder problems, pay close attention to what is given versus what is needed. If you are given the diameter instead of the radius, divide by 2 first. If you need the total surface area but are given the volume and height, first solve for the radius using the volume formula, then apply the surface area formula. Also note whether a problem asks for lateral area only or total surface area, as they are different quantities.
steps: Identify the given measurements: radius r, diameter d, or height h
If given the diameter, convert to radius: r = d/2
For volume: V = πr²h; substitute and calculate
For lateral surface area: L = 2πrh; this is just the curved side
For total surface area: S = 2πr² + 2πrh or S = 2πr(r + h)
Include correct units: cubic units for volume, square units for area

examples.title: Volume and Surface Area of a Cylinder
examples.text: Find the volume and total surface area of a cylinder with radius 5 cm and height 12 cm. Volume V = π(5)²(12) = 300π ≈ 942.48 cm³. Lateral area L = 2π(5)(12) = 120π ≈ 376.99 cm². Total surface area S = 2π(5)(5 + 12) = 2π(5)(17) = 170π ≈ 534.07 cm². The total area includes both circular bases and the curved side.

examples.title: Finding Radius from Volume
examples.text: A cylinder has a volume of 200π cm³ and a height of 8 cm. Find its radius. Using V = πr²h: 200π = πr²(8). Divide both sides by 8π: r² = 25. Take the square root: r = 5 cm. Now find the lateral area: L = 2π(5)(8) = 80π ≈ 251.33 cm².

lessons.tip: The formula S = 2πr(r + h) is the most efficient way to remember total surface area. Factor out 2πr and you get both terms: 2πr × r (both bases) plus 2πr × h (lateral area).

quiz.q: What is the volume of a cylinder with radius 4 cm and height 10 cm? (Leave in terms of π)
What is the lateral surface area of a cylinder with radius 3 m and height 7 m? (Leave in terms of π)
quiz.explanation: L = 2πrh = 2π(3)(7) = 42π m². This is the area of just the curved side.

quiz.q: A cylinder has diameter 14 cm and height 10 cm. What is its total surface area? (Use π ≈ 22/7)

lessons.title: Pyramids
lessons.description: Find surface area and volume of pyramids.
vocabulary: Pyramid — a 3D solid with a polygonal base and triangular lateral faces meeting at an apex
Apex — the single point where all lateral triangular faces of a pyramid meet
Base area (B) — the area of the polygonal base of the pyramid
Slant height (l) — the height of each triangular lateral face (along its altitude)
Height (h) — the perpendicular distance from the apex to the base plane
Regular pyramid — a pyramid with a regular polygon base and congruent isosceles triangular faces
Lateral faces — the triangular sides connecting the base edges to the apex
lessons.formula:
Volume: V = ⅓Bh

Lateral Area (regular pyramid): L = ½Pl
  (P = base perimeter, l = slant height)

Total Surface Area: S = L + B = ½Pl + B

B = area of the base
h = pyramid height (perpendicular to base)
l = slant height (height of triangular face)

Note: V = ⅓Bh (one-third, not one-half!)
lessons.content:
A pyramid is a three-dimensional solid with a single polygonal base and triangular lateral faces that all meet at a point called the apex. The most familiar is the square pyramid (like the Great Pyramid of Giza), but pyramids can have triangular, pentagonal, hexagonal, or any polygonal base. The volume of every pyramid follows the same formula: V = ⅓Bh, where B is the base area and h is the perpendicular height.

The lateral surface area of a regular pyramid is L = ½Pl, where P is the perimeter of the base and l is the slant height (the height of each triangular face, not the pyramid height). For a regular square pyramid, each lateral face is a congruent triangle with base equal to a side of the square base and height equal to the slant height l. The total surface area is S = ½Pl + B, adding the base area.

A critical distinction is between the pyramid height h (perpendicular to the base) and the slant height l (along the triangular face). These are different measurements connected by the Pythagorean theorem: l² = h² + (s/2)² for a regular pyramid, where s is a base side length. Always check which height a problem gives you before applying formulas. The volume formula uses h, and the lateral area formula uses l.
steps: Identify the shape of the base and calculate its area B
Find the base perimeter P
Identify the pyramid height h (for volume) and the slant height l (for lateral area)
Calculate volume: V = ⅓Bh (remember the one-third factor!)
Calculate lateral area: L = ½Pl (use slant height, not pyramid height)
Calculate total surface area: S = L + B = ½Pl + B

examples.title: Square Pyramid Volume and Surface Area
examples.text: A regular square pyramid has a base side of 10 cm, pyramid height 12 cm, and slant height 13 cm. Base area B = 10 × 10 = 100 cm². Base perimeter P = 4 × 10 = 40 cm. Volume V = ⅓(100)(12) = 400 cm³. Lateral area L = ½(40)(13) = 260 cm². Total surface area S = 260 + 100 = 360 cm².

examples.title: Finding Slant Height from Pyramid Height
examples.text: A regular square pyramid has base side 8 m and pyramid height 3 m. Find the slant height. The slant height, pyramid height, and half the base side form a right triangle: l² = h² + (s/2)² = 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25. So l = 5 m. Now find the lateral area: L = ½Pl = ½(32)(5) = 80 m².

lessons.tip: The most common mistake with pyramids is forgetting the 1/3 in V = ⅓Bh. Remember: a pyramid has one-third the volume of a prism with the same base and height. Think of it as 'one-third the base area times the height.'

quiz.q: What is the volume of a pyramid with base area 45 cm² and height 8 cm?
quiz.explanation: V = ⅓Bh = ⅓(45)(8) = ⅓(360) = 120 cm³. Remember the one-third factor.
