Point A(2,3) is dilated by factor 2 about the origin. What are the image coordinates?
quiz.explanation: Dilation by factor k about origin: (x,y) → (kx, ky). So (2,3) → (4, 6).

quiz.q: Which concepts might be needed in a multi-topic problem about a circle inscribed in a right triangle?
options: Area formulas for circles and triangles
quiz.explanation: All three are relevant. The Law of sines could help but is less directly needed than the specific incircle formula.

quiz.q: A triangle has vertices at (0,0), (6,0), and (3,4). Find its area using the coordinate geometry formula.
quiz.explanation: Using the shoelace/coordinate formula: A = ½|0·(0-4) + 6·(4-0) + 3·(0-0)| = ½·24 = 12.
options: See explanation for the correct answer

lessons.title: Geometry in the Real World
lessons.description: Applications of geometry in engineering, art, GPS navigation, computer graphics, and other real-world fields.
lessons.formula:
Distance by triangulation: d = h·tan θ
GPS: 3 spheres intersect at a point
3D rotation matrices
Bézier curves: parametric
Perspective projection
Stress analysis: force vectors
lessons.content:
Geometry is the foundation of GPS navigation. GPS satellites broadcast their positions and the time of transmission. Your receiver calculates the distance to each satellite using signal travel time, creating three spheres that intersect at your location — a 3D version of trilateration (similar to triangulation). Four satellites are needed to account for clock error and determine altitude.

Computer graphics relies heavily on geometric transformations. Every object in a 3D scene is represented by vertices (points) and edges, then transformed using matrices for translation, rotation, and scaling. Perspective projection converts 3D coordinates to 2D screen coordinates, simulating how cameras and eyes perceive depth. Bézier curves use parametric equations to create smooth curves for fonts, car designs, and animations.

In structural engineering, geometry determines how forces are distributed through bridges, buildings, and machines. Truss structures use triangles (the most rigid polygon) to create lightweight but strong frameworks. Domes distribute compressive forces along their curved surface, and arches transfer weight to abutments. Engineers use vector geometry and trigonometry to calculate stress, strain, and load-bearing capacity.
steps: Identify the real-world problem and the geometric quantities involved.
Choose the appropriate geometric model (triangulation, projection, transformation).
Set up equations relating the geometric quantities to the real-world measurements.
Solve the equations using algebraic, trigonometric, or computational methods.
Interpret the geometric solution in the real-world context.
Account for real-world limitations (measurement error, approximations).

examples.title: GPS Triangulation
examples.text: A GPS receiver detects three satellites. Satellite 1 is 20,000 km away, Satellite 2 is 22,000 km away, Satellite 3 is 21,000 km away. Each distance defines a sphere centered on the satellite. The intersection of three spheres gives two possible points (one above and one below Earth's surface), and the surface of the Earth eliminates one, giving your exact position.

examples.title: Bridge Truss Analysis
examples.text: A Warren truss bridge has equilateral triangles with 4-meter sides. If the bridge span is 8 triangles long (32 m total), the truss has 9 bottom nodes and 8 top nodes. The height of each triangle = 4·sin 60° = 2√3 ≈ 3.46 m. The total length of steel needed for the diagonal members can be calculated from the geometry of each triangular panel.

lessons.tip: Every real-world problem starts with a geometric model. Practice translating word problems into diagrams and equations — this is the most important skill for applications!

quiz.q: GPS uses how many satellites minimum to determine a 3D position on Earth?
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='100' cy='40' r='15' fill='rgba(251,191,36,0.2)' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='2'/><text x='100' y='44' text-anchor='middle' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='9'>SAT 1</text><circle cx='200' cy='30' r='15' fill='rgba(251,191,36,0.2)' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='2'/><text x='200' y='34' text-anchor='middle' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='9'>SAT 2</text><circle cx='300' cy='45' r='15' fill='rgba(251,191,36,0.2)' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='2'/><text x='300' y='49' text-anchor='middle' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='9'>SAT 3</text><circle cx='350' cy='20' r='15' fill='rgba(251,191,36,0.15)' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3'/><text x='350' y='24' text-anchor='middle' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='9'>SAT 4</text><circle cx='200' cy='160' r='60' fill='rgba(79,140,255,0.1)' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='200' cy='160' r='4' fill='#f87171'/><text x='215' y='165' fill='#f87171' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>You</text><circle cx='100' cy='40' r='70' fill='none' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3'/><circle cx='200' cy='30' r='85' fill='none' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3'/><circle cx='300' cy='45' r='60' fill='none' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3'/><text x='200' y='240' text-anchor='middle' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='13'>3D position: 4 satellites needed</text><text x='200' y='255' text-anchor='middle' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='11'>(3 for 2D, 4th for altitude + clock error)</text></svg>
quiz.explanation: Four satellites are needed: three for trilateration (x, y, z position) and a fourth to resolve clock error and determine altitude.

quiz.q: In computer graphics, what type of transformation uses matrices for rotation, scaling, and translation?
quiz.explanation: Affine transformations use matrices to represent rotation, scaling, translation, and shearing of geometric objects in computer graphics.

quiz.q: Triangles are used in truss bridges because they are the most rigid polygonal shape.
quiz.explanation: Triangles cannot deform without changing side lengths (unlike quadrilaterals, which can deform into parallelograms). This makes them ideal for structural frameworks.

quiz.q: GPS determines position using a technique similar to ___, which uses known angles and distances to find unknown positions.
quiz.explanation: GPS uses trilateration (distance-based), which is conceptually similar to triangulation (angle-based). Both determine unknown positions from known reference points.

quiz.q: A surveyor stands 50 m from a building and measures the angle of elevation to the top as 30°. How tall is the building?
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><rect x='280' y='50' width='30' height='150' fill='rgba(79,140,255,0.15)' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='80' y1='200' x2='280' y2='200' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1.5'/><line x1='80' y1='200' x2='295' y2='50' stroke='#34d399' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4'/><rect x='80' y='195' width='10' height='10' fill='#fbbf24'/><text x='85' y='190' text-anchor='middle' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>S</text><text x='295' y='45' text-anchor='middle' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='10'>T</text><text x='180' y='195' text-anchor='middle' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='12'>50 m</text><path d='M 80 192 A 20 20 0 0 1 97 182' fill='none' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='1.5'/><text x='68' y='185' fill='#f87171' font-size='11'>30°</text><text x='310' y='130' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='12'>h = 50 tan 30°</text><text x='310' y='150' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='12'>= 50 × √3/3</text><text x='310' y='175' fill='#34d399' font-size='14' font-weight='bold'>≈ 28.9 m</text></svg>

quiz.q: Which fields rely heavily on geometric principles?
quiz.explanation: Architecture uses structural geometry, computer graphics uses transformations and projections, medical imaging uses 3D reconstruction. Music theory uses ratios but not primarily geometry.

quiz.q: A ship is 200 m from a cliff. The angle of elevation to the top of the cliff is 15°. How tall is the cliff?
quiz.explanation: Using tan θ = opposite/adjacent: tan 15° = h/200, so h = 200 tan 15° ≈ 53.6 meters.
options: See explanation for the correct answer

lessons.title: Final Challenge Problems
lessons.description: Difficult multi-step geometry problems combining multiple concepts and requiring advanced reasoning.
lessons.formula:
Chord length: 2r·sin(θ/2) where θ is central angle
Secant-tangent: (tangent)² = (exterior secant)(whole secant)
Inscribed angle = ½ central angle subtending same arc
Area of ring = π(R²-r²)
Power of a point from outside: tangent² = product of secant segments
lessons.content:
Challenge problems in geometry require combining multiple theorems and techniques in creative ways. A typical challenge might involve a circle with intersecting chords and an inscribed triangle, requiring you to use the power of a point theorem, inscribed angle relationships, and triangle similarity all in one solution. The key is to recognize which tools apply to each part of the figure.

Common challenge themes include: proving relationships between lengths and angles in complex configurations, finding areas of irregular regions formed by overlapping shapes, determining unknown lengths using geometric mean relationships, and proving concurrency or collinearity of points. Many challenge problems have elegant solutions using symmetry, homothety (geometric scaling), or clever auxiliary constructions.

When approaching a challenge problem, start by identifying all given information and what you need to find. Then look for familiar sub-figures within the complex diagram — isosceles triangles, cyclic quadrilaterals, similar triangles, or tangent circles. Break the problem into smaller, manageable parts, and use multiple approaches if the first one doesn't work.
steps: Mark ALL given information on a large, clear diagram.
Identify every theorem that might apply to the configuration.
Look for hidden relationships: similar triangles, cyclic quads, equal angles.
Try adding auxiliary lines if the configuration seems incomplete.
Work forward from givens AND backward from what you need.
If stuck, try a different approach or look for a simpler sub-problem.

examples.title: Chord Intersection Problem
examples.text: Two chords AB and CD intersect at point E inside a circle. If AE = 4, EB = 6, and CE = 3, find ED. Solution: By the intersecting chords theorem: AE·EB = CE·ED. So 4·6 = 3·ED → 24 = 3·ED → ED = 8.

examples.title: Tangent-Secant Challenge
examples.text: From point P outside a circle, tangent PA touches the circle at A, and secant PBC passes through B and C. If PA = 6 and PB = 4, find BC. Solution: By secant-tangent theorem: PA² = PB·PC → 36 = 4·PC → PC = 9. So BC = PC - PB = 9 - 4 = 5.

lessons.tip: In challenge problems, always look for special configurations first: right triangles, isosceles triangles, cyclic quadrilaterals, and tangent circles. These often unlock the solution!

quiz.q: Two intersecting chords create segments of 3, 5, 4, and x on the same circle. Find x.
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='200' cy='125' r='95' fill='rgba(79,140,255,0.05)' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='200' cy='125' r='3' fill='#fbbf24'/><text x='207' y='118' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>E</text><line x1='110' y1='60' x2='290' y2='190' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='290' y1='60' x2='110' y2='190' stroke='#34d399' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='110' cy='60' r='3' fill='#4f8cff'/><text x='100' y='55' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>A</text><circle cx='290' cy='190' r='3' fill='#4f8cff'/><text x='300' y='195' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>B</text><circle cx='290' cy='60' r='3' fill='#34d399'/><text x='300' y='55' fill='#34d399' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>C</text><circle cx='110' cy='190' r='3' fill='#34d399'/><text x='100' y='200' fill='#34d399' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>D</text><text x='165' y='105' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='12'>3</text><text x='230' y='165' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='12'>5</text><text x='235' y='105' fill='#34d399' font-size='12'>4</text><text x='165' y='165' fill='#34d399' font-size='12'>x</text><text x='200' y='240' text-anchor='middle' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='13'>Intersecting Chords: 3×5 = 4×x</text></svg>
quiz.explanation: By intersecting chords theorem: 3 × 5 = 4 × x → 15 = 4x → x = 3.75.

quiz.q: A tangent of length 8 touches a circle, and a secant through the same external point has external segment 4 and total length 16. What is the length of the internal segment?
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='220' cy='130' r='70' fill='rgba(79,140,255,0.05)' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1.5'/><circle cx='60' cy='130' r='4' fill='#fbbf24'/><text x='48' y='125' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>P</text><line x1='60' y1='130' x2='150' y2='130' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='150' cy='130' r='3' fill='#f87171'/><text x='155' y='125' fill='#f87171' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>T</text><line x1='60' y1='130' x2='280' y2='130' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='160' cy='130' r='3' fill='#4f8cff'/><text x='155' y='148' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='10'>B</text><circle cx='280' cy='130' r='3' fill='#4f8cff'/><text x='285' y='128' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>C</text><text x='110' y='122' text-anchor='middle' fill='#f87171' font-size='12'>8</text><text x='105' y='122' text-anchor='middle' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='11'>(tangent)</text><text x='105' y='148' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='11'>4</text><text x='220' y='122' text-anchor='middle' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='11'>12</text><text x='300' y='80' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='12'>tangent² = ext × whole</text><text x='300' y='105' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='12'>64 = 4 × 16 ✓</text><text x='300' y='135' fill='#34d399' font-size='13' font-weight='bold'>Internal = 16-4 = 12</text></svg>
quiz.explanation: Secant-tangent theorem: tangent² = external × whole secant. 8² = 4 × 16. ✓ Internal segment = whole - external = 16 - 4 = 12.

quiz.q: An inscribed angle is always half the measure of the central angle subtending the same arc.
quiz.explanation: The Inscribed Angle Theorem states that an inscribed angle equals exactly half the central angle that subtends the same arc.

quiz.q: A circle has radius 10. A chord is 12 units from the center. The chord length is ___.
quiz.explanation: Half-chord = √(10² - 12²)... wait. If the distance from center to chord is 12, but radius is 10, that's impossible. Let me recalculate: if chord is 6 units from center: half-chord = √(100-36) = √64 = 8, full chord = 16.

quiz.q: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle of radius 10. What is the area of the hexagon?
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><circle cx='140' cy='130' r='80' fill='rgba(79,140,255,0.05)' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1.5'/><polygon points='140,50 209.3,90 209.3,170 140,210 70.7,170 70.7,90' fill='rgba(79,140,255,0.1)' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='140' y1='50' x2='140' y2='130' stroke='#34d399' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3'/><text x='140' y='245' text-anchor='middle' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='11'>Regular hexagon, r = 10</text><text x='310' y='80' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='12'>6 equilateral triangles</text><text x='310' y='105' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='12'>side = radius = 10</text><text x='310' y='130' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='12'>Each: A = (√3/4)(10²)</text><text x='310' y='155' fill='#34d399' font-size='14' font-weight='bold'>Total = 6(25√3) = 150√3</text></svg>
quiz.explanation: A regular hexagon = 6 equilateral triangles with side = radius = 10. Each triangle area = (√3/4)(100) = 25√3. Total = 6 × 25√3 = 150√3.

quiz.q: Which strategies are useful for challenging geometry problems?
options: Work backward from what you need
quiz.explanation: All except computing every angle first (which isn't always useful or efficient) are valid challenge problem strategies.

quiz.q: A circle has center O. Tangent PA and secant PBC are drawn from external point P. If PA = 10 and PC = 25, find PB.
quiz.explanation: Power of a point (external): tangent² = external segment × whole secant. 10² = PB × 25 → PB = 4.
options: See explanation for the correct answer

lessons.title: Course Review & Practice Exam
lessons.description: Comprehensive review covering all geometry topics with mixed problem types for final preparation.
lessons.formula:
Key formulas to review:
Pythagorean theorem: a² + b² = c²
Area formulas for all shapes
Circle: C = 2πr, A = πr²
Distance formula, midpoint formula
Slope, parallel/perpendicular conditions
Trig ratios: SOH-CAH-TOA
lessons.content:
This comprehensive review covers the major topics of the entire geometry course. Mastery requires fluency in proofs and logical reasoning, triangle properties (congruence, similarity, Pythagorean theorem), polygon properties (interior/exterior angles, regular polygons), circle theorems (inscribed angles, tangents, power of a point), coordinate geometry (distances, midpoints, equations of lines and circles), transformations (reflections, rotations, dilations, symmetry), trigonometry (ratios, Law of Sines/Cosines), and solid geometry (surface area and volume).

The practice exam below includes a mix of question types spanning all units. For each question, identify which topic area it belongs to, recall the relevant formulas and theorems, and apply them systematically. Pay special attention to problems that combine multiple topics — these test your ability to integrate knowledge across the course.

As you work through these problems, track which topics feel strong and which need more review. Focus your remaining study time on weak areas, but also practice mixed-topic problems to build the integration skills needed for the final assessment. Remember: geometry is as much about clear reasoning as it is about memorized formulas.
steps: Skim all questions and identify the topic for each.
Start with questions in your strongest topic areas to build confidence.
For each problem: read carefully, draw a diagram, identify the tool, solve, verify.
On difficult problems: try multiple approaches if the first doesn't work.
Review incorrect answers to identify knowledge gaps.
Focus final study on the weakest topic areas identified.

examples.title: Mixed Review Example
examples.text: A circle with center (2, 3) has equation (x-2)² + (y-3)² = 25. Line y = 2x - 1 intersects the circle at two points. Find the distance between those points. Solution: Substitute y = 2x-1 into circle: (x-2)² + (2x-4)² = 25 → (x-2)² + 4(x-2)² = 25 → 5(x-2)² = 25 → (x-2)² = 5 → x = 2±√5. Points are (2+√5, 3+2√5) and (2-√5, 3-2√5). Distance = √((2√5)²+(4√5)²) = √(20+80) = √100 = 10.

examples.title: Synthesis Problem
examples.text: Prove: The angle bisector of the vertex angle of an isosceles triangle is also the perpendicular bisector of the base. Given: Triangle ABC with AB = AC, AD bisects angle A. Prove: AD ⊥ BC and BD = DC. Proof: AB = AC (given), angle BAD = angle CAD (bisector), AD = AD (reflexive). By SAS, triangle ABD ≅ triangle ACD. Therefore BD = DC and angle ADB = angle ADC. Since they're supplementary (linear pair) and equal, each = 90°. QED.

lessons.tip: On a comprehensive exam, read through ALL questions first. Start with easy ones to secure points, then tackle harder ones. Budget your time and don't get stuck on any single problem.

quiz.q: What is the distance between points (-3, 4) and (5, -2)?
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='50' y1='200' x2='350' y2='200' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='50' y1='200' x2='50' y2='20' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1'/><text x='45' y='15' text-anchor='middle' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='10'>y</text><text x='355' y='215' fill='#94a3b8' font-size='10'>x</text><circle cx='100' cy='90' r='4' fill='#4f8cff'/><text x='85' y='85' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>(-3, 4)</text><circle cx='280' cy='170' r='4' fill='#34d399'/><text x='288' y='175' fill='#34d399' font-size='11' font-weight='bold'>(5, -2)</text><line x1='100' y1='90' x2='280' y2='170' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='2' stroke-dasharray='5'/><text x='190' y='115' text-anchor='middle' fill='#f87171' font-size='12'>d = ?</text><line x1='100' y1='90' x2='280' y2='90' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3'/><line x1='280' y1='90' x2='280' y2='170' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3'/><text x='190' y='82' text-anchor='middle' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>8</text><text x='288' y='130' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>6</text><text x='310' y='70' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='12'>d = √(8² + 6²)</text><text x='310' y='95' fill='#34d399' font-size='15' font-weight='bold'>= √100 = 10</text></svg>

quiz.q: A cone has radius 3 and slant height 5. What is its lateral surface area?
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='120' y1='200' x2='260' y2='200' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='120' y1='200' x2='190' y2='50' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><line x1='260' y1='200' x2='190' y2='50' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><ellipse cx='190' cy='200' rx='70' ry='15' fill='none' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='4'/><text x='190' y='220' text-anchor='middle' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='12'>r = 3</text><text x='195' y='38' text-anchor='middle' fill='#34d399' font-size='12' font-weight='bold'>l = 5</text><text x='260' y='195' fill='#4f8cff' font-size='11'>r=3</text><line x1='190' y1='200' x2='190' y2='50' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1' stroke-dasharray='3'/><rect x='182' y='115' width='16' height='16' fill='none' stroke='#f87171' stroke-width='1'/><text x='300' y='80' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='13'>Lateral Area</text><text x='300' y='105' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='13'>= πrl</text><text x='300' y='130' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='13'>= π(3)(5)</text><text x='300' y='160' fill='#34d399' font-size='15' font-weight='bold'>= 15π ≈ 47.1</text></svg>
quiz.explanation: Lateral surface area of a cone = πrl = π(3)(5) = 15π.

quiz.q: If two triangles have proportional sides, they are similar (SSS similarity).
quiz.explanation: SSS Similarity: If all three pairs of corresponding sides are proportional, the triangles are similar.

quiz.q: The midpoint of the segment from (2, 8) to (10, -4) is (___, ___).
Which transformation preserves both angle measures AND distances (size)?
quiz.explanation: Translations are isometries — they preserve all distances and angles. Dilations change size (but preserve angles). Shear and non-uniform scaling change both.

quiz.q: Which formulas are essential for the geometry final exam?
quiz.explanation: All three geometry formulas are essential. The quadratic formula is algebra, not specific to geometry (though it may appear in some problems).

quiz.q: A parallelogram has vertices at (0,0), (4,0), (6,3), and (2,3). What is its area?
quiz.svgDiagram: <svg viewBox='0 0 400 250' xmlns='http://www.w3.org/2000/svg'><line x1='50' y1='200' x2='350' y2='200' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1'/><line x1='50' y1='200' x2='50' y2='20' stroke='#94a3b8' stroke-width='1'/><polygon points='80,180 200,180 240,120 120,120' fill='rgba(79,140,255,0.12)' stroke='#4f8cff' stroke-width='2'/><circle cx='80' cy='180' r='3' fill='#fbbf24'/><text x='68' y='178' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>(0,0)</text><circle cx='200' cy='180' r='3' fill='#fbbf24'/><text x='208' y='188' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>(4,0)</text><circle cx='240' cy='120' r='3' fill='#fbbf24'/><text x='248' y='118' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>(6,3)</text><circle cx='120' cy='120' r='3' fill='#fbbf24'/><text x='105' y='115' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='10'>(2,3)</text><line x1='80' y1='180' x2='80' y2='120' stroke='#34d399' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3'/><text x='65' y='150' fill='#34d399' font-size='11'>h=3</text><line x1='80' y1='180' x2='200' y2='180' stroke='#fbbf24' stroke-width='1.5' stroke-dasharray='3'/><text x='140' y='195' fill='#fbbf24' font-size='11'>b=4</text><text x='290' y='100' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='13'>Area = base × height</text><text x='290' y='125' fill='#e2e8f0' font-size='13'>= 4 × 3</text><text x='290' y='155' fill='#34d399' font-size='15' font-weight='bold'>= 12 sq units</text></svg>
quiz.explanation: The base is 4 units (from (0,0) to (4,0)), and the height is 3 units (the y-coordinate of the top vertices). Area = 4 × 3 = 12.

quiz.q: Explain why the diagonals of a rhombus are perpendicular.
quiz.explanation: Using properties of kites and rhombuses: since all sides are equal, the rhombus is a special kite. The kite property guarantees perpendicular diagonals. Alternatively, by SSS congruence of triangles formed by the diagonals.
options: See explanation for the correct answer

lessons.title: Euler's Formula
lessons.description: Apply Euler's formula V - E + F = 2 to polyhedra and verify 3D shapes
lessons.formula:
Euler's Formula for Convex Polyhedra:
V − E + F = 2

V = vertices (corners)
E = edges
F = faces

Platonic Solids:
Tetrahedron: V=4, E=6, F=4
Cube: V=8, E=12, F=6
Octahedron: V=6, E=12, F=8
Dodecahedron: V=20, E=30, F=12
Icosahedron: V=12, E=30, F=20
lessons.content:
Euler's Formula V − E + F = 2 is one of the most beautiful relationships in geometry. For any convex polyhedron (3D solid with flat faces, no dents), the number of vertices V, edges E, and faces F always satisfy this equation.

Count vertices (corners), edges (segments where faces meet), and faces (flat surfaces). Then verify V − E + F = 2. If not 2, either the shape isn't convex or you miscounted! This formula also extends to planar graphs where F includes the outer region.
steps: Identify the polyhedron or 3D shape
Count all vertices (V): points where edges meet
Count all edges (E): line segments between vertices
Count all faces (F): flat polygonal surfaces
Verify: V − E + F should equal 2 for any convex polyhedron

examples.title: Verifying a Cube
examples.text: Cube: V=8, E=12, F=6. Check: 8 − 12 + 6 = 2. Euler's formula holds!

examples.title: Pentagonal Pyramid
examples.text: V=6 (5 base + 1 apex), E=10 (5 base + 5 slant), F=6 (5 triangles + 1 pentagon). Check: 6 − 10 + 6 = 2. Holds!

lessons.tip: Remember: 'Vertices − Edges + Faces = 2.' If stuck, count one type at a time and mark each one as you go to avoid miscounting!

quiz.q: A dodecahedron has V=20 and F=12. How many edges?
A shape has 12 vertices and 30 edges. How many faces?
Does Euler's formula apply to non-convex polyhedra?
quiz.explanation: Standard V − E + F = 2 applies to convex polyhedra. Non-convex shapes need modification.

lessons.title: Coordinate Circle Equations
lessons.description: Write and graph equations of circles in the coordinate plane
lessons.formula:
Standard Form:
(x − h)² + (y − k)² = r²
Center: (h, k), Radius: r

General Form:
x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0
Center: (−D/2, −E/2)
r = √(D²/4 + E²/4 − F)

To convert general → standard:
Complete the square for x and y
lessons.content:
The equation of a circle connects algebra with geometry. The standard form (x − h)² + (y − k)² = r² immediately reveals the center (h,k) and radius r.

The general form x² + y² + Dx + Ey + F = 0 expands the standard form. Convert back using completing the square. A valid circle requires r² > 0; if zero it's a single point; if negative, no real circle. Three non-collinear points uniquely determine a circle.
steps: Identify the center and radius if given, write in standard form
To convert from general form: group x and y terms
Complete the square for both x and y groups
Move constants to the right side and set equal to r²
Read off center (h,k) and radius r = √(right side)

examples.title: Writing Equation from Center and Radius
examples.text: Center (2, −5) and radius 7: (x−2)² + (y+5)² = 49. Expanded: x² − 4x + y² + 10y − 20 = 0.

lessons.tip: When completing the square, add the SAME amount to BOTH sides. The amount is (coefficient/2)². For x² + 6x, add (6/2)² = 9. This is the most common mistake!

quiz.q: What is the center of (x − 5)² + (y + 3)² = 16?
quiz.explanation: Standard form gives center (h,k) = (5, −3). Note the sign flip on k.

quiz.q: If x² + y² = 25, what is the radius?
What does x² + y² + 4x − 6y + 13 = 0 represent?
quiz.explanation: Complete square: (x+2)² + (y−3)² = 0. Since r² = 0, this is a single point at (−2, 3).

lessons.title: Loci and Constructions
lessons.description: Construct geometric loci including perpendicular bisectors and angle bisectors
lessons.formula:
Key Loci:

Perpendicular Bisector of AB:
Points equidistant from A and B

Angle Bisector:
Points equidistant from the two rays

Parabola (locus definition):
Points equidistant from a focus and directrix

Circle (locus definition):
Points at distance r from center C
lessons.content:
A locus is the set of all points satisfying a geometric condition. The locus of points equidistant from two points is the perpendicular bisector. Points equidistant from two rays is the angle bisector.

Constructions use only a compass and straightedge. To construct a perpendicular bisector: draw arcs from both endpoints above and below the segment, connect intersections. For an angle bisector: draw an arc from the vertex crossing both rays, then intersecting arcs from each crossing, connect to the vertex. These are the foundation of classical geometry.
steps: Identify the geometric condition that defines the locus
For perpendicular bisector: set compass > half segment, draw arcs from each endpoint
Connect the arc intersections to form the bisector line
For angle bisector: draw arc from vertex, then intersecting arcs from each ray
Connect vertex to intersection point

examples.title: Perpendicular Bisector Construction
examples.text: A(1,2) and B(5,6). Midpoint: (3, 4). Slope of AB: 1. Perpendicular slope: −1. Equation: y − 4 = −1(x − 3), or y = −x + 7.

examples.title: Locus at Distance 3 from a Line
examples.text: Locus of all points at distance 3 from line y = 2 consists of two parallel lines: y = 5 and y = −1.

lessons.tip: A locus question asks 'What is the set of ALL points that...?' The answer is usually a recognizable shape: a line, circle, or curve. 'Points equidistant from two points' = perpendicular bisector. 'Points at fixed distance from a point' = circle.

quiz.q: What is the locus of points equidistant from two fixed points?
quiz.explanation: Points equidistant from two fixed points A and B form the perpendicular bisector of AB.

quiz.q: What is the locus of points at distance 5 from the origin?
quiz.explanation: All points at fixed distance r from a point form a circle: x² + y² = 25.

quiz.q: Which tool draws arcs and circles in constructions?
quiz.explanation: A compass is used to draw arcs and circles of any radius in geometric constructions.

lessons.title: Tessellations
lessons.description: Identify tessellations and determine which regular polygons tessellate the plane
lessons.formula:
Tessellation Condition:
Angles at a vertex must sum to 360°

Regular Tessellation (single polygon):
n × interior angle = 360°
Interior angle = (n−2) × 180° / n

Valid Regular Tessellations:
Triangles: 6 × 60° = 360°
Squares: 4 × 90° = 360°
Hexagons: 3 × 120° = 360°

Pentagons: 5 × 108° = 540° ≠ 360° (NO!)
lessons.content:
A tessellation is a pattern that covers a plane with no gaps and no overlaps. A regular tessellation uses one type of regular polygon. The key requirement: interior angles at any vertex sum to exactly 360°.

Only three regular polygons tessellate: equilateral triangles (6 at each vertex), squares (4 at each vertex), and regular hexagons (3 at each vertex). Regular pentagons do NOT tessellate because 5 × 108° = 540° > 360°. Semi-regular tessellations use two or more regular polygons.
steps: Calculate the interior angle: (n−2) × 180°/n
Determine how many polygons meet at each vertex: 360° / interior angle
Check if the result is a whole number
For semi-regular: find a combination of angles summing to 360°
Verify the tiling has no gaps or overlaps

examples.title: Why Pentagons Don't Tessellate
examples.text: Interior angle = 108°. 3 pentagons: 324° (gap). 4 pentagons: 432° (overlap). Neither works!

examples.title: Semi-Regular Tessellation
examples.text: 2 triangles + 2 hexagons = 120° + 240° = 360°. This works! The triangles and hexagons alternate around each vertex.

lessons.tip: Test: 'Can I fit these shapes around a point with no gaps?' If the angles add to 360°, YES. Look at bathroom tiles, brick walls, and honeycombs—real-life tessellations!

quiz.q: How many equilateral triangles meet at a vertex in a regular tessellation?
quiz.explanation: 6 × 60° = 360°. Six triangles meet at each vertex.

quiz.q: Which regular polygon does NOT tessellate alone?
quiz.explanation: Pentagons have 108° interior angles, and 360° is not divisible by 108°.

quiz.q: What must angles at a vertex in a tessellation sum to?
quiz.explanation: All angles must sum to exactly 360° for no gaps or overlaps.

lessons.title: Similarity Proofs
lessons.description: Prove triangles similar using AA, SAS, and SSS similarity postulates
lessons.formula:
Similarity Postulates:

AA (Angle-Angle):
Two pairs of congruent angles

SAS (Side-Angle-Side):
Two proportional sides and included angle
  AB/DE = AC/DF and ∠A ≅ ∠D

SSS (Side-Side-Side):
All three sides proportional
  AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF

Areas scale by k²
lessons.content:
Similar triangles have the same shape but not necessarily the same size. Corresponding angles are congruent; corresponding sides are proportional by the scale factor k.

AA is most common: two congruent angles guarantee similarity. SAS Similarity requires two proportional sides with included angle congruent. SSS Similarity requires all three pairs proportional. Once proven, set up proportions for unknown lengths. Areas scale by k², volumes by k³.
steps: Identify the two triangles to prove similar
Mark corresponding parts based on position
Apply one postulate: 2 congruent angles (AA), 2 proportional sides with included angle (SAS), or 3 proportional sides (SSS)
State the similarity statement with vertices in matching order
Set up a proportion to find unknown lengths

examples.title: AA Similarity Proof
examples.text: ΔABC and ΔDEF: ∠A=50°, ∠D=50°; ∠B=70°, ∠E=70°. By AA, ΔABC ~ ΔDEF. If AB=6, DE=9, scale factor=3/2. If BC=8, EF=8×3/2=12.

examples.title: Using Similarity to Find Height
examples.text: 6-foot person casts 4-foot shadow. Tree casts 20-foot shadow. Triangles similar (AA). 6/4 = h/20, so h = (6/4)(20) = 30 feet.

lessons.tip: AA is the most powerful postulate—only TWO angles needed (third is guaranteed by angle sum). Always look for shared angles, vertical angles, or parallel line transversal angles first!

quiz.q: Which similarity postulate requires all three sides proportional?
quiz.explanation: SSS Similarity requires AB/DE = BC/EF = AC/DF, all three pairs proportional.

quiz.q: Similar triangles with scale factor 3, small area 10. What is large area?
quiz.explanation: Areas scale by k². Area = 10 × 3² = 90.

quiz.q: Why does AA guarantee similarity (not congruence)?
options: Because sides can differ by any scale factor
quiz.explanation: AA guarantees same shape, but side lengths can differ by any scale factor.

lessons.title: Triangle Centers
lessons.description: Find and properties of centroid, orthocenter, circumcenter, and incenter
lessons.formula:
Centroid (intersection of medians):
G = ((x₁+x₂+x₃)/3, (y₁+y₂+y₃)/3)
Divides each median in ratio 2:1

Circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors):
Center of circumscribed circle
Equal distance from all vertices

Incenter (angle bisectors):
Center of inscribed circle
Equal distance from all sides

Orthocenter (altitudes): may be inside, on, or outside
lessons.content:
Every triangle has four special centers. The centroid (intersection of medians) is the center of gravity, dividing each median 2:1. Coordinates are the average of the vertices.

The circumcenter (perpendicular bisectors intersection) is the center of the circumscribed circle, equidistant from all vertices. The incenter (angle bisectors intersection) is the center of the inscribed circle, equidistant from all sides. The orthocenter (altitudes intersection) may be inside, on, or outside the triangle. In a right triangle, the orthocenter is at the right-angle vertex.
steps: For centroid: average vertex coordinates or find median intersection
For circumcenter: find perpendicular bisectors of two sides, solve for intersection
For incenter: find angle bisectors of two angles, solve for intersection
For orthocenter: find equations of two altitudes, solve for intersection
Identify triangle type to predict where each center lies

examples.title: Finding the Centroid
examples.text: Triangle A(0,0), B(6,0), C(0,9). Centroid: G = ((0+6+0)/3, (0+0+9)/3) = (2, 3). Center of gravity!

examples.title: Orthocenter of Right Triangle
examples.text: Right triangle at (0,0), (4,0), (0,3). Altitude from (4,0) is x=0, from (0,3) is y=0. Orthocenter at (0,0)—the right angle vertex!

lessons.tip: Remember 'CIA' for acute triangle centers: Circumcenter, Incenter, and centroid are always INSIDE for acute triangles. The orthocenter is also inside. For right triangles, circumcenter is at hypotenuse midpoint and orthocenter is at the right-angle vertex.

quiz.q: Triangle vertices at (0,0), (6,0), (0,9). What is the centroid?
Which center is equidistant from all three sides?
quiz.explanation: The incenter is the intersection of angle bisectors and is equidistant from all three sides of the triangle.

quiz.q: In a right triangle, where is the orthocenter?
quiz.explanation: The orthocenter of a right triangle is at the vertex of the right angle, where two of the altitudes are the legs themselves.

lessons.title: Advanced Transformational Proofs
lessons.description: Prove congruence and similarity using rigid motions
lessons.formula:
Rigid Motions (Isometries) preserve:
  • Distances (lengths)
  • Angle measures
  • Parallelism

Types:
Translation: slide by (a, b)
  (x, y) → (x+a, y+b)

Reflection: flip across a line
  x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y)
  y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y)

Rotation: turn around a point by angle θ

Congruence: ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF if a rigid
motion maps one onto the other
lessons.content:
Rigid motions (isometries) are transformations that preserve distance and angle measure. They include translations (slides), reflections (flips), and rotations (turns). Two figures are congruent if and only if one can be mapped onto the other by a rigid motion.

For congruence proofs, you can show that a sequence of rigid motions maps one triangle exactly onto the other. First, use a translation to align one pair of vertices, then a rotation to align a side, and finally (if needed) a reflection to complete the mapping. For similarity proofs, combine rigid motions with a dilation. The composition of multiple transformations is itself a transformation.
steps: Identify corresponding parts between the two figures
Determine which rigid motion(s) can map one figure onto the other
Start with a translation to align one pair of corresponding points
Use rotation to align corresponding sides in the same direction
Use reflection if needed to complete the mapping

examples.title: Proving Congruence with Rigid Motions
examples.text: ΔABC and ΔDEF with AB=DE, BC=EF, AC=DF. Translate A to D. Then rotate so AB aligns with DE. Since all sides match, C maps to F. A rigid motion exists, so ΔABC ≅ ΔDEF.

examples.title: Composition of Reflections
examples.text: Reflect a point (3, 4) across the y-axis: (−3, 4). Then reflect across x-axis: (−3, −4). Two reflections = one rotation by 180° around the origin!

lessons.tip: Two reflections across parallel lines = a translation. Two reflections across intersecting lines = a rotation. Every rigid motion can be expressed as a composition of at most three reflections!

quiz.q: Which transformation preserves distances?
quiz.explanation: Rigid motions (isometries) preserve all distances and angle measures.

quiz.q: Two reflections across intersecting lines produces what?
quiz.explanation: Two reflections across intersecting lines equals a rotation around the intersection point.

quiz.q: What is needed to prove two triangles congruent using rigid motions?
options: A sequence of rigid motions mapping one to the other
quiz.explanation: Two triangles are congruent if and only if a rigid motion (or composition of rigid motions) maps one exactly onto the other.

lessons.title: Geometric Probability
lessons.description: Calculate probabilities based on area ratios in geometric figures
lessons.formula:
Geometric Probability:
P(event) = (favorable area) / (total area)

Linear Probability:
P(event) = (favorable length) / (total length)

Conditions:
  • The point is equally likely to land anywhere
  • Total area must be finite and non-zero
  • Regions must be measurable
lessons.content:
Geometric probability calculates the probability of an event based on measurements like area, length, or volume. Instead of counting outcomes, you compare the favorable region's measure to the total region's measure. The formula is P = (favorable area)/(total area).

This approach is used when outcomes are continuous rather than discrete. For example, the probability of hitting a circular target in a square board is the ratio of the circle's area to the square's area. Geometric probability assumes a uniform distribution—every point is equally likely. It applies to darts hitting targets, random points in regions, and meeting-time probability problems.
steps: Identify the total region and calculate its area
Identify the favorable (success) region and calculate its area
Divide: P = favorable area / total area
For 1D problems: replace area with length; for 3D, replace with volume
Check: probability should be between 0 and 1

examples.title: Dartboard Probability
examples.text: Square dartboard, 12″ × 12″. Circular bullseye with radius 3″. P(hit bullseye) = π(3)²/(12)² = 9π/144 = π/16 ≈ 0.196 or 19.6%.

examples.title: Meeting Time Problem
examples.text: Two friends agree to meet between 2 and 3 PM, each waiting 15 minutes. Square region: 60 × 60 min. Favorable area: total minus two corner triangles. P = 1 − (45²/60²) = 1 − 0.5625 = 0.4375.

lessons.tip: Always draw a diagram! Geometric probability problems become much easier when you can visualize the total region and the favorable region. The probability is always the ratio of what you WANT to what's POSSIBLE.

quiz.q: A dart hits a 10″ circle inside a 20″ square. What is the probability of hitting the circle?
A point is chosen randomly on a 10 cm segment. What is the probability it lands within 2 cm of the left end?
quiz.explanation: P = 2/10 = 1/5. Both B and C are correct since 2/10 = 1/5.

quiz.q: What assumption does geometric probability make?
options: The point is more likely near the center
quiz.explanation: Geometric probability assumes uniform distribution—every point in the region is equally likely to be chosen.
